q: In an experiment, live and boiled yeast cells are compared in Congo red. The live cells remain unstained, while the boiled cells become stained. Which explanation best links these observations?
opts: Live yeast cells break down the dye, while boiling causes them to start producing it.
The selectively permeable membrane of live yeast cells prevents the dye from entering, while boiling destroys it.
Boiled yeast cells have smaller dye molecules, so these pass more easily through the intact membrane.
Live yeast cells let the dye through, but it does not stain them, while boiled cells keep it outside.
why: A live yeast cell remains unstained because its selectively permeable membrane does not let the dye through. Boiling destroys the membrane, so the dye enters. The observation does not mean that yeast cells break down or produce the dye.

s: Since the membrane of live yeast cells lets water through, it must also let Congo red molecules through.
why: The membrane lets water through because water molecules are very small, but it does not let the larger Congo red molecules through. The trap is to assume that letting water through means letting all substances through.

q: What is the name of the property of the membrane of live yeast cells that lets water through but prevents large Congo red molecules from entering?
why: The membrane is selectively permeable because it lets different substances through to different degrees. It is not equally permeable to all substances.

text: After the yeast cells are boiled, the membrane [retains|loses] its selective permeability, so Congo red enters the cells.
opts: loses
retains
gains
why: Boiling destroys the membrane, so it loses its selective permeability and the dye can enter. The trap is to think that boiling preserves or increases its selectivity.

q: A semi permeable membrane separates two solutions. One side has fewer dissolved substances than the other. In which direction will water move?
opts: Towards the side with fewer dissolved substances, because there is more water there.
Towards the side with more dissolved substances, because there is less water there.
Towards the side with more dissolved substances, together with most of the solute.
Equally in both directions, since a semi permeable membrane does not let water through.
why: Water moves by osmosis towards the side with the higher concentration of dissolved substances. The trap is to confuse the direction in which water moves with that of the solute.

s: If one side of a semi permeable membrane has more dissolved substances, water will move towards that side by osmosis.
why: Water moves from a place with a higher water concentration to one with a lower water concentration, that is, towards the higher concentration of dissolved substances.

q: Which description does not belong to osmosis?
items: The movement of water through a semi permeable membrane.
The movement of solvent, but not solute.
The movement of water towards a higher concentration of dissolved substances.
The movement of solute through a membrane towards a higher concentration of solute.
why: In osmosis, water moves through a semi permeable membrane, not solute. The last description confuses which substance moves and the direction in which it moves.

q: What is the name of the type of diffusion in which water moves through a semi permeable membrane towards the side with more dissolved substances?
why: The description links the movement of water through a semi permeable membrane with its movement towards a higher concentration of dissolved substances.

q: A cell is moved from solution X to solution Y. Solution X has more dissolved substances than the cell, while solution Y has fewer. How should the two solutions be described?
opts: X is hypotonic and Y is hypertonic relative to the cell.
Both X and Y are hypertonic relative to the cell.
X is hypertonic and Y is hypotonic relative to the cell.
Both X and Y are hypotonic relative to the cell.
why: A hypertonic solution has more dissolved substances than the cell, while a hypotonic solution has fewer. The concentrations must be compared relative to the cell.

s: Distilled water is hypotonic to a cell because it has fewer dissolved substances than the cell.
why: A hypotonic solution has a lower concentration of dissolved substances than the cell. Distilled water is given as an example of such a solution.

q: What is the name of a solution that has a lower concentration of dissolved substances than the cell?
why: A lower concentration of dissolved substances than in the cell means the environment is hypotonic.

q: A plant cell is placed in an environment from which water moves out of the cell. Which outcome is characteristic of plasmolysis?
opts: The vacuole gets bigger and the membrane presses against the cell wall.
The vacuole shrinks and the cell wall moves in with it.
The vacuole and protoplast shrink, and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
Water enters the cell and the cell contents press against the cell wall.
why: During plasmolysis, the cell loses water, so the vacuole and protoplast shrink and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall. The cell wall stays in place.

q: Which phenomenon is not one of the changes associated with plasmolysis?
items: The vacuole shrinks as it loses water.
The membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
The cell wall shrinks along with the vacuole.
why: During plasmolysis, the vacuole and protoplast shrink, while the cell wall stays in place. The incorrect option says that the cell wall shrinks too.

s: During plasmolysis, the plant cell wall shrinks along with the vacuole, so the membrane stays against it.
why: The vacuole and protoplast shrink, while the cell wall stays in place, so the membrane pulls away from it. The statement incorrectly says that the cell wall shrinks.

q: A plant cell that has been in a salty solution is moved into distilled water. Which outcome best describes the change?
opts: Water enters the cell and vacuole, turgor pressure develops, and the cell gradually returns to its original shape.
Water leaves the cell and vacuole, the membrane pulls away from the wall, and the cell gradually returns to its original shape.
Water enters the cell, but the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall.
Water leaves the cell, the vacuole gets bigger, and the cell wall prevents turgor pressure from developing.
why: Distilled water is hypotonic relative to the contents of the cell, so water enters the cell and vacuole. The resulting turgor pressure pushes against the cell wall, and the cell returns to its original state.

s: When a plant cell takes in water in a hypotonic environment, turgor pressure can develop because of the rigid cell wall, without the cell bursting.
why: Water enters the plant cell and fills the vacuole, creating pressure against the cell wall. The trap is to assume that swelling must cause the cell to burst.

q: What process gradually returns a plant cell to its original shape after the environment changes from hypertonic to hypotonic?
why: Deplasmolysis is the reverse of plasmolysis, in which the cell gradually returns to its original shape.

q: An animal cell is moved into a solution with a lower concentration of dissolved substances than the cell. What is the most likely outcome?
opts: Water leaves the cell, so it shrinks and wrinkles.
Water enters the cell, so it swells and may burst.
Water enters the cell, but the cell wall prevents it from bursting.
Water leaves the cell, and the vacuole creates turgor pressure.
why: An environment with a lower concentration of dissolved substances is hypotonic, so water enters the animal cell. As it has no protective cell wall, it may swell and burst.

s: In a hypertonic environment, an animal cell shrinks because water moves out of the cell into the environment.
why: A hypertonic environment has more dissolved substances than the cell, so water leaves the cell and it shrinks. The trap would be to confuse the direction of water movement with that in a hypotonic environment.

q: Which does not belong when describing the response of an animal cell in a hypotonic environment?
items: Turgor pressure develops against the cell wall.
why: An animal cell in a hypotonic environment takes in water, swells and may burst. Turgor pressure against the cell wall is associated with plant cells, which have a cell wall.

q: Salt is sprinkled on the roots of a weed. Which sequence of changes best explains why the plant wilts?
opts: The surroundings become hypotonic, water enters the root cells, the cells undergo plasmolysis and the plant wilts.
The surroundings become hypertonic, water leaves the root cells, the cells undergo plasmolysis and the plant wilts.
The surroundings become hypertonic, water enters the root cells, the cells return to their original state and the plant wilts.
The surroundings become hypotonic, water leaves the root cells, the cells undergo plasmolysis and the plant wilts.
why: Salt increases the concentration of dissolved substances around the roots, so the surroundings become hypertonic. Water leaves the cells, which undergo plasmolysis, and the plant wilts.

text: Based on the experiment with plant cells in a 10% salt solution, we conclude that the surroundings are [hypotonic|hypertonic].
opts: hypertonic
hypotonic
isotonic
why: The salt solution has a higher concentration of dissolved substances than the cell, so it is hypertonic. The trap is to choose a hypotonic environment, in which water would enter the cell.

q: Which one does not belong among the changes in a plant cell transferred from water to a 10% salt solution?
items: The membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
The cell returns to its original state.
why: In a hypertonic solution, the cytoplasm shrinks, the chloroplasts become more concentrated and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall. Returning to the original state describes transfer to a hypotonic environment, such as distilled water.

q: Onion cells are first in a 10% salt solution and are then transferred to distilled water. What do we expect after the transfer?
opts: Water leaves the cells, the cytoplasm shrinks further and the membrane moves away from the wall.
Water enters the cells, the membrane moves back towards the wall and the cell gradually returns to its original state.
Water enters the cells, the vacuole shrinks and the membrane moves even further away from the wall.
Water leaves the cells, the vacuole grows and the cell gradually returns to its original state.
why: Distilled water is hypotonic, so water enters the cells that were previously in a hypertonic salt solution. This is deplasmolysis, and the cell gradually returns to its original state.

q: In an experiment, the membrane allows water through but not dyes. Which conclusion best explains this observation?
opts: The membrane is selectively permeable, as it allows some substances through but not others.
The membrane is impermeable, as water must pass through it without any restrictions.
The membrane allows all substances through, but the dye cannot enter because of the water.
The membrane allows only dissolved substances through, while water stays outside the cell.
why: The membrane allows different substances through selectively. It allows water through but not some dissolved substances. The trap is to conclude that being permeable to water also means being permeable to dye.

s: If the plasma membrane allows water through, it must also allow many dissolved substances through.
why: The plasma membrane allows water through but not many dissolved substances. The false statement confuses permeability to water with general permeability.

q: Which one does not belong among the properties of a selectively permeable membrane?
items: It allows some substances through but not others.
It allows water through but not many dissolved substances.
It regulates the movement of substances through the membrane.
It allows all substances through equally, regardless of their type.
why: Selective permeability means that the membrane allows different substances through to different extents, thereby regulating their movement. The fourth option incorrectly assumes that all substances pass through equally.

q: A substance moves without using energy from an area where its concentration is higher to an area where it is lower. Which type of movement is this?
opts: Active transport, because the substance moves between areas with different concentrations.
Osmosis, because any movement of a substance down a concentration difference involves water.
Passive transport, because the substance moves from a higher to a lower concentration without using energy.
Active transport, because the membrane always uses energy when substances move through it.
why: Movement from a higher to a lower concentration without using energy is passive transport. The trap is to confuse the direction of passive and active transport.

s: During passive transport, a substance can move without using energy from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration.
why: Passive transport occurs from a higher to a lower concentration and does not require energy. Movement from a lower to a higher concentration is characteristic of active transport.

q: What is the movement of a substance from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration called, when no energy is needed?
why: The description combines both characteristics of passive transport: movement down a concentration difference and no use of energy. Active transport occurs in the opposite direction and requires energy.

q: A substance moves from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration. Which description best fits this example?
opts: It is passive transport, which occurs without energy through channel proteins.
It is active transport, in which a membrane pump uses energy.
It is passive transport, in which a carrier protein uses energy.
It is selective permeability, in which the substance always moves down the concentration difference.
why: Movement from a lower to a higher concentration goes against the concentration gradient, so it requires energy and is carried out by membrane pumps. The trap is to confuse passive transport with active transport.

q: Which one does not belong among the characteristics of active transport?
items: A substance moves from a lower to a higher concentration.
Energy is needed for the movement of the substance.
Movement occurs with the help of membrane pumps.
A substance moves from a higher to a lower concentration without energy.
why: The first three options describe active transport. The fourth describes passive transport, so it is different, even though it also involves movement through a membrane.

s: Membrane ion pumps carry out active transport, in which a substance moves against the concentration gradient and therefore requires energy.
why: Active transport occurs from a lower to a higher concentration, is carried out by membrane pumps and requires energy. The trap would be to say that energy is not needed, which is true of passive transport.

q: In the same experiment, substance X moves from a higher to a lower concentration without using energy, while substance Y moves from a lower to a higher concentration using energy. How should we classify the two cases?
opts: X is transported actively, while Y is transported passively.
X and Y are both transported passively, as they both move through a membrane.
X is transported passively, while Y is transported actively.
X and Y are both transported actively, as their concentrations differ.
why: X moves from a higher to a lower concentration without using energy, so this is passive transport. Y moves from a lower to a higher concentration using energy, so this is active transport. The trap is to classify both cases in the same way just because they both involve a membrane.

q: A description of a cell includes both the liquid part and the cell organelles. Which term includes both parts?
opts: Cytosol, because it includes the liquid and the organelles.
Cytoplasm, because it includes the liquid and the organelles.
Dissolved substances, because they include the liquid and the organelles.
Water, because it includes the liquid and the organelles.
why: The cytoplasm consists of the cytosol and the cell organelles. The cytosol is only its liquid part.

s: If the cell organelles are removed from the cytoplasm, its liquid part, the cytosol, remains.
why: The cytosol is the liquid part of the cytoplasm, which also contains cell organelles.

q: The description covers only the liquid part of the cytoplasm, which is mostly water with dissolved proteins, fats and salts. Which term matches the description?
opts: Cytosol, because it is the liquid part of the cytoplasm.
Cytoplasm, because it is the liquid part without organelles.
Cell organelles, because they are dissolved substances.
Cell membrane, because it is the liquid part of the cell.
why: The description matches the cytosol, which is the liquid part of the cytoplasm and contains dissolved substances. The cytoplasm also includes cell organelles.

q: Which one does not belong in the same group as the other terms listed?
why: Proteins, fats and salts are substances dissolved in the cytosol. The cytosol is the liquid part of the cytoplasm, not one of these dissolved substances.

q: Which term refers to the whole made up of the cytosol and cell organelles?
why: The cytoplasm consists of the cytosol together with the cell organelles. Cytosol alone refers only to its liquid part.

q: In a diagram, label X covers the liquid part of the cell and the cell organelles, while label Y covers only the liquid part. Which explanation of the labels is correct?
opts: X is the cytosol, Y is the cytoplasm.
X is the cytoplasm, Y is the cytosol.
X is the dissolved substances, Y is the cytoplasm.
X is the cell organelles, Y is the cytosol.
why: The cytoplasm includes the cytosol and cell organelles, while the cytosol is only the liquid part. The trap is to confuse the broader term with the narrower one.

s: Because the cytosol consists mostly of water, proteins, fats and salts cannot be part of its composition.
why: In addition to water, proteins, fats and salts are also dissolved in the cytosol. The statement wrongly concludes that the presence of water excludes other substances.

q: A researcher wants to describe a cell in a way that captures its two fundamental roles. Which statement expresses this best?
opts: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living things.
A cell is the basic structural unit, which has no functional role.
A cell is a functional unit, but is not a structural unit of living things.
A cell is a unit that transfers hereditary information only between different living things.
why: A cell is both the basic structural and functional unit of living things. The trap is in answers that leave out or change one of these two roles.

q: Which term refers to the basic structural and functional unit of living things?
why: A cell is defined as the basic structural and functional unit of living things.

s: If we consider a cell to be the basic structural unit of living things, we have described only one of its two fundamental roles.
why: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit, so the statement correctly identifies the structural role as just one of the two.

q: After cell division, a parent cell and a daughter cell are formed. Which direction of hereditary information transfer is supported by the importance of cell division?
opts: From the daughter cell to the parent cell.
From the parent cell to the daughter cell.
From one daughter cell to another parent cell.
From the parent cell to another parent cell.
why: Cell division enables hereditary information to be transferred from the parent cell to the daughter cell. The trap is reversing the direction of transfer.

s: The importance of cell division is the transfer of hereditary information from the daughter cell to the parent cell.
why: The direction is reversed: hereditary information is transferred from the parent cell to the daughter cell.

text: Cell division enables hereditary information to be transferred from the [daughter|parent] cell to the daughter cell.
opts: parent
daughter
eukaryotic
why: The correct direction of transfer is from the parent cell to the daughter cell. The trap is switching the roles of the two cells.

q: When classifying cells by their internal structure, you are looking at a bacterial cell. Which group do you choose?
opts: Eukaryotic cells, because bacteria are eukaryotes.
Prokaryotic cells, because bacteria are prokaryotes.
Eukaryotic cells, because bacteria have a true nucleus and organelles.
Prokaryotic cells, because bacteria belong to fungi, plants and animals.
why: Bacterial cells are prokaryotic. The trap is switching the groups or classifying bacteria as fungi, plants or animals.

q: Which one does not belong?
why: Bacterial cells are prokaryotic, whereas fungal, plant and animal cells are eukaryotic. The trap is that all the cells listed are from living things, but they do not belong to the same structural group.

s: If a description of a cell mentions a true nucleus and organelles, we classify it as a eukaryotic cell based on its structure.
why: Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and organelles. Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus.

text: Based on their structure, bacterial cells are [eukaryotic|prokaryotic] cells.
opts: prokaryotic
eukaryotic
functional
why: Bacterial cells are prokaryotic. The trap is confusing them with the cells of fungi, plants and animals, which are eukaryotic.

q: A sample contains two groups of cells. Cells in group A are mostly 4 µm in size, while cells in group B are 35 µm. Which explanation matches the usual size ranges given?
opts: The size of group A is typical of prokaryotic cells, while that of group B is typical of eukaryotic cells.
The size of group A is typical of eukaryotic cells, while that of group B is typical of prokaryotic cells.
The sizes of both groups are typical of prokaryotic cells.
The sizes of both groups are typical of eukaryotic cells.
why: 4 µm falls within the usual size range of most prokaryotic cells, while 35 µm falls within that of most eukaryotic cells. The trap is switching the size ranges of the two groups.

q: Which statement does not match the usual size range of prokaryotic cells?
why: The range from 10 to 100 µm is given for eukaryotic cells. The other statements fall within the usual size range of prokaryotic cells.

q: A cell is found to have one circular DNA molecule that is not associated with proteins. Which description best matches this finding?
opts: The hereditary material of a prokaryotic cell.
The hereditary material of a eukaryotic cell.
The hereditary material of a eukaryotic cell, with one linear DNA molecule.
The hereditary material of a prokaryotic cell, with several linear DNA molecules.
why: A prokaryotic cell is characterised by one circular DNA molecule that is not associated with proteins. The trap is attributing a linear shape or several molecules to prokaryotes.

s: If DNA is associated with specific proteins and consists of numerous linear molecules, the description is consistent with a eukaryotic cell.
why: Eukaryotic cells have numerous linear DNA molecules associated with specific proteins. Prokaryotic DNA is one circular molecule and is not associated with proteins.

q: Which type of cell is described by numerous linear DNA molecules associated with specific proteins?
why: Numerous linear DNA molecules associated with specific proteins are characteristic of eukaryotic cells. One circular DNA molecule not associated with proteins is characteristic of prokaryotes.

q: Researchers cannot find a nucleus or a nuclear envelope in a cell. Which conclusion is consistent with the material?
opts: The cell is eukaryotic, because a nuclear envelope is not always present.
The cell is prokaryotic, because it has no nucleus or nuclear envelope.
The cell is eukaryotic, because it has a nucleus without a nuclear envelope.
The cell is prokaryotic, because it has a nucleus but no nuclear envelope.
why: A prokaryotic cell has neither a nucleus nor a nuclear envelope. A eukaryotic cell has both, so the options that assume a nucleus are incorrect.

q: Which statement is not a characteristic of a eukaryotic cell?
items: It has numerous linear DNA molecules.
It has no nucleus or nuclear envelope.
why: A eukaryotic cell has a nucleus and a nuclear envelope. The absence of both is characteristic of a prokaryotic cell.

s: The nuclear envelope is a characteristic of prokaryotic cells, since they have no nucleus.
why: Prokaryotic cells have neither a nucleus nor a nuclear envelope, whereas eukaryotic cells have both. The trap is concluding that the absence of a nucleus means that an envelope is present.

q: What is the name of the envelope that the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell has, but a prokaryotic cell does not?
why: The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus, which eukaryotic cells have. Prokaryotic cells have neither a nucleus nor a nuclear envelope.

q: When observing cell division, researchers find that the spindle does not take part. Which description best fits this observation?
opts: A prokaryotic cell divides by binary fission.
A eukaryotic cell divides by mitosis.
A eukaryotic cell divides by meiosis.
A eukaryotic cell divides without a spindle.
why: Prokaryotic cells divide by binary fission without a spindle. Mitosis and meiosis are ways eukaryotic cells divide, and both involve a spindle.

s: If a spindle takes part in cell division, the division may be mitosis or meiosis.
why: Eukaryotic cells divide using a spindle, by either mitosis or meiosis. A trap would be to attribute either of these types of division to a prokaryotic cell.

q: Which description fits least with the others if they are grouped according to whether a spindle takes part in division?
items: Prokaryotic binary fission without a spindle
why: The first three descriptions involve a spindle, while the fourth describes prokaryotic division without one. The trap is to focus on all the descriptions being related to cell division.

q: A cell has larger ribosomes, ER, a Golgi apparatus and mitochondria, but no plastids. Which explanation best fits this information?
opts: It could be a eukaryotic cell that is not a plant cell.
It must be a prokaryotic cell without organelles.
It must be a plant cell with plastids.
It could be a prokaryotic cell with larger ribosomes.
why: Larger ribosomes, ER, a Golgi apparatus and mitochondria are features of eukaryotes, while plants have plastids. The trap is to conclude that all eukaryotes must have plastids.

q: Which type of cell is described by small ribosomes and the absence of ER, a Golgi apparatus, mitochondria and plastids?
why: Prokaryotes have smaller ribosomes and lack the membrane-bound organelles listed. Larger ribosomes and these organelles are associated with eukaryotic cells.

s: A plant eukaryotic cell may have plastids, whereas eukaryotic cells in other groups do not have them.
why: The learning material lists plastids in plants, while eukaryotes have larger ribosomes, ER, a Golgi apparatus and mitochondria. The trap is to confuse a feature of plant cells with a feature of all eukaryotes.

q: In an experiment, one substance from the surroundings enters a cell, while another does not. Which explanation best links this observation to the role of the cell membrane?
opts: The membrane is selectively permeable and regulates the cell's interaction with its surroundings.
The membrane is completely permeable and allows all substances to pass through.
The membrane is impermeable and prevents any interaction with the surroundings.
The membrane stores genetic information and therefore selects which substances pass through.
why: The selective permeability of the membrane means that it regulates the cell's interaction with its surroundings. The trap is to confuse selective permeability with complete permeability or impermeability.

s: Molecule transport and waste removal are among the functions carried out by structures in the cell.
why: The learning material lists molecule transport and waste removal among the functions of cell structures. A trap would be to claim that their functions include only energy conversion or the storage of genetic information.

text: The cell is surrounded by a [completely permeable|selectively permeable] biological membrane, which regulates its interaction with its surroundings.
opts: selectively permeable
completely permeable
impermeable
why: The correct phrase is “selectively permeable”, because the membrane regulates the cell's interaction with its surroundings. The trap is to confuse selective permeability with allowing all substances through or with impermeability.

q: Which option does not describe a function of cell structures listed in the learning material about eukaryotic cell structure?
items: Transfer of hereditary information from a parent cell to a daughter cell
why: Transfer of hereditary information from a parent cell to a daughter cell is listed as the importance of cell division, not as one of the functions of cell structures in this learning material. The other options are among the listed functions of cell structures.

q: A student describes living things by mentioning cells but not cell products. Which judgement best fits the cell theory?
opts: The description is incomplete, because living things are made up of cells and cell products.
The description is correct, because cell theory mentions only cells, not their products.
The description is incomplete, because cell products replace cells in the composition of living things.
The description is correct only if cells arose spontaneously from non-living matter.
why: Cell theory states that all living things are made up of cells and cell products. The trap is to leave out cell products.

q: A new cell appears in a sample, but researchers do not detect any existing cell dividing. Which conclusion is consistent with cell theory?
opts: The new cell arose spontaneously, since no existing cells divided.
The observation conflicts with the claim that new cells arise only by division of existing cells.
The observation confirms that hereditary information is formed only after cell division.
The new cell arose from non-living matter, which is the usual way cells form.
why: According to cell theory, new cells can arise only by division of existing cells. A new cell appearing without any detected division is therefore not consistent with this claim.

s: According to cell theory, a cell's hereditary information contains instructions for the growth, functioning and development of cells.
why: Cell theory links hereditary information with instructions for the growth, functioning and development of cells. The statement does not confuse the role of hereditary information with the role of cell division.

q: Which statement does not belong among the stated aspects of cell theory?
items: All living things are made up of cells and cell products.
New cells arise only by division of existing cells.
Chemical reactions important for life take place in cells.
Living organisms can arise spontaneously from non-living matter.
why: The first three statements are consistent with cell theory. Spontaneous generation from non-living matter was a belief that Pasteur disproved.

text: Before cell theory, people believed that living organisms arose {spontaneously} from {non-living matter}.
why: Before cell theory, people supported the idea that living organisms arose spontaneously from non-living matter. The division of existing cells expresses the opposite explanation for how new cells arise.

q: A researcher wants to explain why it became possible to study cells and microorganisms systematically. Which role of the microscope best fits this aim?
opts: The microscope opened up the fields of cell biology and microbiology and enabled the development of cell theory.
The microscope proved that living organisms arise from non-living matter, thereby establishing cell theory.
The microscope enabled new cells to arise without division and thereby gave rise to microbiology.
The microscope showed that hereditary information forms only after a cell starts to divide.
why: The development of the microscope opened up a new area of research, cell biology and microbiology, and is closely linked to the development of cell theory. The other options attribute to it claims that are not listed as part of its importance.

s: The development of the microscope was closely linked to the development of cell theory, but did not open up new areas of research.
why: The microscope was linked to the development of cell theory and opened up the fields of cell biology and microbiology. The statement wrongly denies its wider significance.

q: A student concludes that the microscope had no important influence on research because cell theory is about cells, not microscopes. Which correction to this reasoning is best supported?
opts: The microscope made it possible to study cells and microorganisms, so it is linked to the development of cell theory.
The microscope replaced cell theory, since it caused new cells to arise.
The microscope is important only for studying hereditary information, not for studying cells.
The microscope proved that cells arise spontaneously, and cell theory later confirmed this.
why: The development of the microscope opened up the study of cells and microorganisms and is closely linked to the development of cell theory. The trap is to conclude that the connection is unimportant simply because the microscope is not a principle of the theory.

q: What is the name of the belief that living organisms arise from non-living matter, which Pasteur disproved?
why: The term for the belief that living organisms arise spontaneously from non-living matter is spontaneous generation. Pasteur disproved it.

q: Which conclusion best expresses what was considered to be true about the origin of new cells after spontaneous generation had been disproved?
opts: New cells arise only by division of existing cells.
New cells arise from non-living matter if there are no other cells in the surroundings.
New cells arise spontaneously when chemical reactions begin.
New cells arise from hereditary information without existing cells dividing.
why: After spontaneous generation was disproved, it was accepted that new cells arise only by division of existing cells. The wrong options reintroduce spontaneous generation or confuse hereditary information with the formation of a cell.

q: An account of an old microscope says that it has several lenses and is focused by changing the distance between them. Which milestone does this description match?
opts: Janssen's compound microscope
Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscope
Hooke's presentation in Micrographia
Leeuwenhoek's discovery of protozoa
why: Janssen's microscope had several lenses, and focusing depended on changing the distance between them. The trap is confusing it with Leeuwenhoek, who made single-lens microscopes.

s: If a microscope is focused by changing the distance between its lenses, its focusing method matches the description of Janssen's microscope.
why: Janssen's compound microscope could be focused by changing the distance between its lenses. This is not a feature attributed in the material to Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes.

q: What do we call a microscope with more than one lens, the first version of which was made by Janssen?
why: A microscope with more than one lens is a compound microscope. The trap is confusing it with Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscope.

q: An account of an old microscope mentions one lens and magnification of up to 270 times. Which description matches these details?
opts: Janssen made the first compound microscope
Leeuwenhoek made single-lens microscopes
Hooke introduced the term cell in Micrographia
Janssen focused the microscope by moving the specimen
why: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes had one lens and achieved magnification of up to 270 times. The trap is confusing the number of lenses with Janssen's compound microscope.

s: Leeuwenhoek made about 500 microscopes, each with more than one lens.
why: Leeuwenhoek made about 500 microscopes with one lens each. The trap is combining the correct number of microscopes with the incorrect detail about the number of lenses.

text: Leeuwenhoek made about {500} microscopes, each with {one} lens.
why: The material states that Leeuwenhoek made about 500 microscopes with one lens each. The number 270 refers to the maximum magnification, not the number of microscopes.

q: In a book published in 1665, a researcher introduced a term for structures in cork. Which researcher and term match this description?
opts: Janssen and the compound microscope
Leeuwenhoek and red blood cells
Hooke and cell
Leeuwenhoek and protozoa
why: In 1665, Hooke introduced the term cell for structures in cork in his book Micrographia. The trap is confusing this with discoveries attributed to Leeuwenhoek.

text: Hooke introduced the term [bacterium|cell] for structures in cork.
opts: cell
protozoan
sperm cell
why: The correct term is cell. Bacteria, protozoa and sperm cells are among the discoveries attributed to Leeuwenhoek in the material.

q: What is the name of the book in which Hooke presented his work on structures in cork in 1665?
why: Hooke presented his work in 1665 in the book Micrographia. The trap is confusing the title of the work with the name of the researcher.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: Hooke's work was presented in Micrographia
why: The first three statements refer to Hooke. The discovery of sperm cells is attributed to Leeuwenhoek in the material.

q: A biologist examines plant and animal tissue and finds that they are made up of groups of cells. Which conclusion is best supported by these findings, according to Schleiden and Schwann?
opts: The cell is the basic unit of living things.
New cells form only by division.
Present-day cells descend from cells of ancient times.
Cells contain instructions for their development.
why: Schleiden and Schwann linked the finding that plants and animals are made up of cells to the conclusion that the cell is the basic unit of living things. The formation of new cells by division was an addition made by Virchow.

s: By 1838/39, Schleiden and Schwann had already included the statement that new cells can form only by division of existing cells.
why: Their cell theory emphasised that plants and animals are made up of groups of cells and that the cell is the basic unit of living things. Virchow later added the statement about the division of existing cells.

q: Which statement is not among the conclusions of Schleiden and Schwann?
items: Plants are made up of groups of cells.
Animals are made up of groups of cells.
The cell is the basic unit of living things.
New cells form by division of existing cells.
why: The first three statements summarise the contribution of Schleiden and Schwann. The last is an addition to cell theory made by Virchow.

q: Which term refers to the basic unit of living things in the conclusion of Schleiden and Schwann?
why: Schleiden and Schwann defined the cell as the basic unit of living things. A likely trap is answering with division, which is part of Virchow's addition.

q: When examining tissue, researchers find that new cells appear when existing cells divide. Which principle of cell theory does this result directly support?
opts: The cell is the basic unit of living things.
Plants and animals are made up of cells.
New cells form by division of existing cells.
Present-day cells are descendants of cells from ancient times.
why: Virchow extended cell theory with the statement that new cells can form only by division of existing cells. The idea that present-day cells descend from cells of ancient times is Weismann's extension.

s: If a researcher claimed that new cells form independently of existing ones, this would be consistent with Virchow's extension of cell theory.
why: Virchow's statement rules out the formation of new cells independently of existing ones, as new cells form only by their division. The trap is reversing how cells form.

q: How do new cells form according to Virchow's extension of cell theory?
why: Virchow argued that new cells can form only by division of existing cells. Saying that they form from non-living matter would confuse this principle with the idea of spontaneous generation.

q: A researcher concludes that all cells living today are descendants of cells from ancient times. Which broader connection did Weismann express with this idea?
opts: A connection between cell theory and evolution.
A connection between cell theory and microscopy.
A connection between cell theory and cell division.
A connection between cell theory and the structure of tissues.
why: By stating that present-day cells descend from cells of ancient times, Weismann connected cell theory with evolution. The idea that existing cells divide was Virchow's, and Weismann built on it.

s: Weismann connected cell theory with evolution by stating that all cells living today are descendants of cells from ancient times.
why: This statement combines Weismann's idea about the origin of present-day cells with the link to evolution. The trap would be to reduce his contribution to the division of existing cells alone.

q: Which statement does not express Weismann's extension of cell theory?
items: Present-day cells descend from cells of ancient times.
Cell theory is connected with evolution.
Present-day cells are descendants of earlier cells.
New cells form only by division of existing cells.
why: The first three statements express Weismann's connection between cell theory, evolution and the origin of present-day cells. The last is Virchow's principle, which Weismann built on.

q: A researcher wants to observe the surface of an opaque object. Which microscope is best suited for this?
opts: TEM, because electrons pass through the specimen.
SEM, because it allows the surface of objects to be observed.
TEM, because electromagnetic lenses direct electrons onto the surface.
SEM, because its short wavelength allows the inside to be observed.
why: An SEM is used to observe the surfaces of objects. The trap is confusing the SEM with features of a TEM, in which electrons pass through the specimen.

s: In an SEM, electrons pass through the specimen, and electromagnetic lenses collect them so that very small structures can be observed.
why: This description combines features of a TEM, not an SEM. An SEM is used to observe the surfaces of objects.

q: Which electron microscope would you choose to observe the surface of an object, rather than electrons passing through a specimen?
why: An SEM is a scanning electron microscope used to observe the surfaces of objects. A TEM, on the other hand, works with electrons that pass through the specimen.

q: Why can very small structures be observed with a TEM?
opts: Because electromagnetic lenses create a vacuum in the column.
Because electrons passing through the specimen do not have a wavelength.
Because an SEM uses the short wavelength of accelerated electrons.
Because accelerated electrons have a short wavelength.
why: The short wavelength of accelerated electrons makes it possible to observe very small structures. Electromagnetic lenses collect the electrons, while a vacuum pump creates the vacuum.

q: Which does not belong among the parts of a TEM?
why: An SEM is a type of electron microscope used to observe surfaces, not a part of a TEM. The other options are listed as parts of a TEM.

q: Which part of a TEM comes after the specimen, before the electrons reach the projector lenses?
opts: condenser lenses
phosphorescent screen
objective lenses
electron gun
why: In a TEM, the objective lenses come after the specimen, followed by the projector lenses. The condenser lenses and electron gun are before the specimen.

q: The breakdown of alcohol and the accumulation of calcium ions increase in a cell. Which organelle is most likely to be more active?
opts: Smooth ER, which is involved in both processes
Rough ER, which is involved in both processes
Ribosomes, which accumulate calcium ions
Golgi apparatus, which breaks down alcohol
why: Smooth ER is involved in breaking down toxic substances, including alcohol, and in accumulating calcium ions. The trap is confusing smooth ER with rough ER, which is involved in producing proteins for secretion and synthesising membranes.

s: If the accumulation of calcium ions in the smooth ER decreased, this could affect signal transmission and muscle contraction.
why: Calcium accumulated in the smooth ER is important for signal transmission and muscle contraction. The statement does not mean that the smooth ER itself causes muscle contraction.

q: Which part of the ER do you associate with the synthesis of lipids and steroids, the breakdown of alcohol and the accumulation of calcium ions?
why: All the listed roles are attributed to the smooth ER. The trap is that rough ER is involved in producing proteins that the cell secretes and in synthesising membranes.

q: A student wants to identify a ribosome by its structure, rather than by its location in the cell or its role. Which description is most helpful?
opts: Made of RNA and proteins, with a larger and a smaller subunit
Made of membranes, with a larger and a smaller cisterna
Made of RNA and lipids, with two equally sized subunits
Made of proteins, with one larger and one smaller membrane
why: A ribosome is made of RNA and proteins and has a larger and a smaller subunit. The trap is confusing ribosomal subunits with membrane structures or assuming that the two subunits are the same size.

q: Which is not among the listed structural features of a ribosome?
items: It has a larger and a smaller subunit
why: A ribosome contains RNA and proteins and is made up of a larger and a smaller subunit. The material identifies the accumulation of calcium ions as a role of the smooth ER.

text: A ribosome consists of a larger and a [larger|smaller] subunit.
opts: smaller
larger
equal in size
why: A ribosome has one larger and one smaller subunit. The trap is repeating the label larger, which would describe the subunits as being the same size.

q: In a microscopic description of a cell, some ribosomes are seen in the cytoplasm and others on the surface of the ER. Which conclusion is consistent with the material?
opts: Ribosomes can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER
Ribosomes can only be free in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes can only be attached to the ER
Ribosomes can be attached to the smooth ER, but not free
why: The material gives both possibilities: ribosomes can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER. The trap is to rule out one of these possibilities.

s: If a cell has ribosomes attached to the ER, it cannot have free ribosomes.
why: Ribosomes in the same cell can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER. The incorrect statement unjustifiably rules out one of the two possibilities given.

text: Ribosomes can be {free} in the cytoplasm or {attached} to the ER.
why: The material describes ribosomes as free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER. The terms embedded and stored do not describe their stated location.

q: In an experiment, ribosomes were observed both in the cytoplasm and on the ER. Which explanation best fits these observations?
opts: Two possible locations of ribosomes in the cell were observed
Ribosomes are on the ER, but not free in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes are in the cytoplasm, while only their subunits are on the ER
Ribosomes are on the ER, and their structure is membranous
why: Ribosomes can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER, so the observations fit both stated possibilities. The trap is unjustifiably concluding that only one location can be correct, or confusing ribosomes with a membrane.

q: A researcher finds that a cellular structure is made of RNA and proteins and has two subunits of different sizes. Which structure have they identified?
opts: A ribosome, made of a larger and a smaller subunit
Rough ER, made of a larger and a smaller subunit
Golgi apparatus, made of a larger and a smaller subunit
Smooth ER, made of a larger and a smaller subunit
why: The structural description matches a ribosome, which contains RNA and proteins and has a larger and a smaller subunit. The trap is confusing the ribosome with an organelle or a membrane structure.

q: A membrane bound structure is found in a cell, where chemical processes take place separately from the cytosol. How should it be classified?
opts: As a cell organelle, because it meets both criteria.
As part of the cytosol, because chemical processes take place in it.
As a ribosome, because it is surrounded by a membrane.
As cisternae, because it is separate from the cytosol.
why: The structure described is an organelle, because it is surrounded by a membrane and the processes within it are separate from the cytosol. The presence of chemical processes or membranes alone does not mean that it is a ribosome or cisternae.

s: A structure surrounded by a membrane is an organelle even when the chemical processes in it are not separate from the cytosol.
why: Both stated features are important for an organelle: being enclosed by a membrane and having processes separate from the cytosol. The statement considers only the membrane and leaves out the second criterion.

q: Which statement does not describe a general feature of cell organelles?
items: Chemical processes take place in them.
Processes in them take place separately from the cytosol.
They are structures surrounded by a membrane.
Ribosomes are always found on their surface.
why: The first three statements describe general features of organelles. Ribosomes on the surface are characteristic of rough ER, but not of all organelles.

q: When observing the ER, you notice membrane-bound spaces of different shapes. Ribosomes are visible on one part of the network, but not on another. Which conclusion is appropriate?
opts: Both parts are rough ER, since they are made up of spaces.
The part with ribosomes is rough ER, and the part without them is smooth ER.
The part without ribosomes is rough ER, and the part with them is smooth ER.
The spaces without ribosomes are not part of the ER because they have no membranes.
why: Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface, whereas smooth ER does not. The different shapes of the spaces do not rule out both parts being ER.

q: What are the flattened, vesicle-like structures that are part of the membrane-bound spaces of the ER called?
why: The flattened, vesicle-like structures of the ER are called cisternae. Tubular spaces are another described form of the ER.

text: The ER is a network of membrane-bound spaces that can be tubular or flattened and vesicle-like. The latter are called {cisternae}. The part of the ER with ribosomes is called {rough ER}.
why: The flattened, vesicle-like structures are cisternae, and the presence of ribosomes on the surface identifies rough ER. Cytosol is not a structure of the ER, and smooth ER does not have ribosomes.

q: A cell needs to make proteins that it will secrete and to renew its membranes. Which function of rough ER is associated with this?
opts: Synthesis of lipids and steroids, and storage of calcium ions.
Breakdown of toxic substances and production of proteins in the cytosol.
Production of proteins for secretion and synthesis of membranes for renewal.
Preparation of products for secretion and budding of vesicles.
why: Rough ER is involved in producing proteins that the cell secretes and in synthesising membranes for renewal. Lipid synthesis and preparation of products for secretion are associated with smooth ER and the Golgi apparatus, respectively.

s: If a cell needs more proteins for secretion, rough ER is involved in producing them.
why: Rough ER is involved in producing proteins that the cell secretes. The trap would be to attribute lipid synthesis to it, since the learning material lists this as a function of smooth ER.

text: Rough ER is involved in producing proteins that the cell secretes and in synthesising [lipids|membranes] for renewal.
opts: membranes
lipids
steroids
why: The correct replacement is “membranes”, since rough ER is involved in synthesising membranes for renewal. Lipids and steroids are associated with the function of smooth ER.

q: Which function is not one of the roles of rough ER?
items: Production of proteins that the cell secretes.
Production of proteins for secretion from the cell.
Synthesis of steroids in the cell.
why: Rough ER is involved in producing proteins for secretion and synthesising membranes for renewal. Steroid synthesis is listed as a function of smooth ER.

q: A membrane network with ribosomes on its surface is observed in a cell. It is involved in producing proteins for secretion. Which additional function is consistent with what is known about this network?
opts: Storage of calcium ions for transmitting signals.
Synthesis of membranes that the cell needs for renewal.
Breakdown of toxic substances such as alcohol.
Synthesis of lipids and steroids in the cell.
why: The network described is rough ER, which, in addition to producing proteins for secretion, is also involved in synthesising membranes for renewal. The other options are listed as functions of smooth ER.

q: A large vacuole in a plant cell is damaged. Which change is directly related to its function?
opts: The cell has more difficulty breaking down substances with digestive enzymes.
The cell loses a space for storing water and part of its support.
The cell can no longer store waste substances.
The cell can no longer produce substances for secretion.
why: A vacuole in a plant cell stores water and provides support to the cell. Breakdown by digestive enzymes is associated with lysosomes, while waste substances are listed in connection with vacuoles in animal cells.

s: A vacuole in a plant cell stores water and substances produced in the cell, but does not provide support to the cell.
why: In addition to storing water and substances, a plant vacuole also provides support to the cell. The incorrect part of the statement is the denial of this function.

q: What are the small vesicles in an animal cell that store water, waste substances and water-soluble dyes called?
why: An animal cell contains several smaller vacuoles that store these substances. The trap is confusing them with a plant cell, which usually has one large vacuole.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: providing support to a plant cell
why: The first three options describe substances stored by vacuoles in animal cells. Providing support is a stated function of the vacuole in a plant cell.

q: If a lysosome no longer contained digestive enzymes, which process would be directly affected?
opts: Storage of water and water-soluble dyes in vesicles.
Production of substances that the cell later secretes.
Breakdown of substances during cellular digestion.
Providing support to the cell by storing water.
why: Digestive enzymes in lysosomes enable the breakdown of substances and take part in cellular digestion. Water storage and support are associated with the vacuole, while the production of substances for secretion is another cellular process.

s: In some plant cells, the vacuole can take over the role of lysosomes.
why: In some plant cells, the vacuole takes over the role of lysosomes. This does not mean that this happens in all plant cells.

q: Name the organelle that is free in the cytoplasm, contains digestive enzymes and takes part in cellular digestion.
why: Lysosomes are free in the cytoplasm and contain digestive enzymes that enable the breakdown of substances. In some plant cells, vacuoles can take over their role, but they are not lysosomes.

q: The cell being observed has several small vesicles containing water, waste substances and water-soluble dyes. Which explanation best fits this observation?
opts: These are vacuoles in an animal cell that store these substances.
This is a vacuole in a plant cell that provides support to the cell.
These are lysosomes that store water and waste substances.
These are vacuoles in a plant cell, which are usually small.
why: Several small vacuoles containing water, waste substances and water-soluble dyes are characteristic of an animal cell. A plant cell usually has one large vacuole, while lysosomes contain digestive enzymes.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: stores waste substances in an animal cell
why: The first three options describe a lysosome. Storing waste substances is listed as a function of vacuoles in animal cells.

q: Ribosomes are present in a cell but are not functioning. Which process would be directly affected?
opts: Preparation of substances secreted by the cell
Protein synthesis
Renewal of the cell membrane
Budding of vesicles from cisternae
why: Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis. Preparation of products for secretion and membranes, as well as vesicle budding, are associated with the Golgi apparatus.

s: If ribosomes in a cell stopped functioning, the preparation of products secreted by the cell would stop directly.
why: Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis, while products for secretion are prepared by the Golgi apparatus. The trap is confusing protein synthesis with their preparation for secretion.

q: An experiment found that certain cell structures carry out protein synthesis. Which structure did they identify?
why: Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes. The question checks the link between a process and an organelle, not its structure.

q: Which feature does not belong in a description of the structure of the Golgi apparatus?
items: The cisternae are arranged in stacks
Ribosomes are attached to the surface
The cisternae form its membrane system
why: The Golgi apparatus is described as a system of flattened membrane cisternae arranged in stacks. Ribosomes on the surface are characteristic of the rough ER, not of the structure of the Golgi apparatus.

text: The membranes of the Golgi apparatus form [tubular|flattened] cisternae arranged in stacks.
opts: flattened
branched
round
why: The Golgi apparatus consists of flattened cisternae arranged in stacks. The option tubular confuses the Golgi apparatus with other forms of membrane-bound spaces.

q: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the structure of the Golgi apparatus from that of the ER?
opts: The Golgi apparatus is a network of tubular spaces, while the ER is a stack of flattened cisternae
The Golgi apparatus consists of stacks of flattened cisternae, while the ER consists of membrane-bound spaces of various shapes
The Golgi apparatus has ribosomes on its surface, while the ER consists of two subunits
The Golgi apparatus consists of two subunits, while the ER consists of stacks of flattened cisternae
why: The Golgi apparatus consists of flattened cisternae arranged in stacks, while the ER is a network of membrane-bound spaces of various shapes. The incorrect options confuse the features of these structures or of ribosomes.

s: Vesicles that bud off from the cisternae at the edges of the outer part of the Golgi apparatus contain substances that it has prepared.
why: Vesicles containing prepared substances bud off from the cisternae at the edges of the outer part of the Golgi apparatus. The statement is correct because it does not attribute the formation of vesicles to ribosomes or the ER.

q: When observing a cell, vesicles are detected budding off from the edge cisternae and containing prepared products for secretion. Which organelle is most likely being observed?
opts: Rough ER
Golgi apparatus
Ribosome
Smooth ER
why: Vesicles containing prepared substances bud off from the edge cisternae of the Golgi apparatus. The rough ER is involved in producing proteins for secretion, but the description of vesicles budding off matches the Golgi apparatus.

q: Which is not among the described functions of the Golgi apparatus?
items: Preparing products that the cell secretes
Preparing membranes to renew the cell membrane
Budding off vesicles containing prepared substances
why: The Golgi apparatus prepares products for secretion and membranes for renewal, and vesicles bud off from its cisternae. Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis.

q: A cell needs substances for secretion and membranes to renew its cell membrane. Which statement best summarises the role of the Golgi apparatus in this case?
opts: It synthesises the substances and stores them in ribosomes
It prepares both types of substance, then vesicles containing them bud off from the cisternae
It breaks down the substances, then vesicles transport them to the cell membrane
It prepares the membranes, while the cisternae themselves synthesise products for secretion
why: The Golgi apparatus prepares products for secretion and membranes for renewal, and vesicles containing them bud off from the cisternae. The distractor is attributing protein synthesis to the Golgi apparatus or to ribosomes.

q: A substance inside the nucleus needs to pass into the cytoplasm. Which nuclear structure connects these two spaces?
opts: The two membranes of the nuclear envelope
Ribosomes on the surface of the envelope
Pores in the nuclear envelope
The nucleolus inside the nucleus
why: Pores in the nuclear envelope connect the inside of the nucleus with the cytoplasm. The membranes and ribosomes are parts of the envelope, while the nucleolus is inside the nucleus.

s: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes, and ribosomes are attached to its surface.
why: Both features of the nuclear envelope are stated in the learning material. The distractor would be confusing ribosomes on the envelope with ribosomes inside the nucleus.

text: The nuclear envelope is made up of [one|two] membranes.
opts: two
three
four
why: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes. The option one is a common confusion with an envelope made up of a single membrane.

q: When observing a cell, you notice that the nucleus is not always in the same place. Which conclusion is consistent with this observation and the learning material?
opts: The nucleus is an independent organelle, but its position in the cell can change.
The nucleus is an independent organelle, so its position in the cell must be fixed.
The nucleus changes position in the cell, so it cannot be considered an independent organelle.
The nucleus is an independent organelle only when its position in the cell does not change.
why: The nucleus is an independent organelle, but its position in the cell changes. The incorrect options confuse being an independent organelle with having a fixed position.

s: Because the nucleus is an independent organelle, its position in the cell is always the same.
why: The learning material states that the position of the nucleus in the cell changes. The distractor assumes that being an independent organelle also means having a fixed position.

q: Which organelle is independent, but can change its position in the cell?
why: The description refers to the nucleus, which the learning material specifically states is an independent organelle whose position in the cell can change.

q: A thread-like network made up of DNA and nuclear proteins is observed in a cell. What is it called, and what happens to it during cell division?
opts: It is chromatin, which forms chromosomes as it coils further.
They are chromosomes, which turn into chromatin as they coil further during division.
They are histones, which bind to DNA and form chromatin during division.
It is chromatin, which uncoils into individual histones during division.
why: DNA and histones together form chromatin, from which chromosomes develop through further coiling during cell division. The incorrect options reverse the direction of the change or confuse chromatin with histones.

q: Which term does not belong when linking the components of chromatin with the structure that forms from it?
why: DNA and histones together form chromatin, and chromosomes develop from chromatin during cell division. The nuclear envelope is not part of this sequence.

text: DNA is associated with nuclear proteins called {histones}; together they form a thread-like network called {chromatin}. During cell division, further coiling turns it into {chromosomes}.
why: Histones are nuclear proteins associated with DNA. Together they form a thread-like network called chromatin, from which chromosomes develop during cell division. Ribosomes and pores do not complete the sequence described.

s: During cell division, chromatin coils further and forms chromosomes.
why: The learning material states that chromosomes form from chromatin through further coiling during cell division. The direction would be reversed if chromatin were said to form from chromosomes.

q: Researchers observe a decrease in cellular respiration in a particular organelle. Which effect is best supported by the notes?
opts: Less ATP and energy are produced in it.
Less chlorophyll and energy are produced in it.
Protein synthesis decreases in it.
The breakdown of toxic substances decreases in it.
why: Cellular respiration in mitochondria is associated with the production of ATP and energy. Protein synthesis and the breakdown of toxic substances are associated with other structures.

s: If cellular respiration decreases in a mitochondrion, ATP production in it may also decrease.
why: Cellular respiration takes place in mitochondria, where ATP is produced. The statement does not confuse this process with photosynthesis in chloroplasts.

q: A cell contains both a mitochondrion and a chloroplast. Which link between an organelle and a process is correct?
opts: Cellular respiration takes place in the mitochondrion, while photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplast.
Photosynthesis takes place in the mitochondrion, while cellular respiration takes place in the chloroplast.
Cellular respiration takes place in both organelles, while photosynthesis takes place in neither.
Photosynthesis takes place in both organelles, while cellular respiration takes place in neither.
why: The notes link cellular respiration with mitochondria and photosynthesis with chloroplasts. The distractor is swapping the processes between the organelles.

q: We are looking for an organelle in a plant cell sample where photosynthesis takes place. Which option best links the group of organelles with the organelle we are looking for?
opts: Plastids are characteristic of plant cells, and chloroplasts are important for photosynthesis.
Plastids are characteristic of plant cells, but photosynthesis takes place in the mitochondrion.
Mitochondria are characteristic of plant cells, and photosynthesis takes place in plastids.
Chloroplasts are similar to mitochondria, so photosynthesis takes place in both organelles.
why: Plastids are characteristic of plant cells, and chloroplasts are the most important plastids because photosynthesis takes place in them. Their similarity to mitochondria does not mean that the same process takes place in both.

q: Which scientific term names the most important plastid, where photosynthesis takes place?
why: The chloroplast is the most important plastid, and photosynthesis takes place in it. It is not a mitochondrion, where cellular respiration takes place.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: Plastids are characteristic of plant cells.
Chloroplasts are the most important plastids.
Cellular respiration takes place in mitochondria.
why: The first three statements describe plastids or chloroplasts. The last one refers to mitochondria and cellular respiration.

q: Which structure does not belong among the listed parts of a chloroplast?
why: Stroma, thylakoids and grana are parts of a chloroplast. The matrix is listed as part of the structure of a mitochondrion.

text: The thylakoid membrane originates from the [outer|inner] membrane of the chloroplast.
opts: outer
inner
both
why: The thylakoid membrane originates from the inner membrane of the chloroplast. The trap is choosing the outer membrane, which surrounds the chloroplast.

q: A researcher compares a chloroplast with an intact inner membrane with one that has no inner membrane. Which conclusion best follows from the notes?
opts: A thylakoid membrane cannot form from the inner membrane in the second chloroplast.
An outer membrane cannot form from thylakoids in the second chloroplast.
Stroma cannot form from grana in the second chloroplast.
Chloroplast DNA cannot form from ribosomes in the second chloroplast.
why: The thylakoid membrane originates from the inner membrane, so it cannot form in the way described if the inner membrane is absent. The other options reverse the direction of origin or confuse different parts of the chloroplast.

s: Thylakoids stacked on top of one another form grana, and a chloroplast also contains DNA and ribosomes.
why: Both statements are consistent with the description of a chloroplast: stacked thylakoids form grana, and the chloroplast also contains DNA and ribosomes. The trap is overlooking that grana are made up of thylakoids.

q: Two cells differ in their characteristics. Which statement best links this difference to the role of the nucleus?
opts: Most DNA is in the nucleus, and its genetic code for proteins is linked to the characteristics of the cell.
The larger and smaller ribosomal subunits are made in the nucleus, and they determine the characteristics of the cell.
The nucleus contains ribosomes and circular DNA, which enable ATP to be produced.
The nucleus is an independent organelle in the cytoplasm where cellular respiration takes place.
why: DNA carries the genetic code for proteins, and the characteristics of a cell depend on this code. Making ribosomal subunits is the role of the nucleolus, while cellular respiration takes place in the mitochondrion.

s: Most DNA is in the nucleus, and its genetic code for proteins is linked to the characteristics of the cell and the living organism made up of those cells.
why: The learning material links the DNA code for proteins to the characteristics of the cell and the living organism. A trap would be to claim that DNA directly carries a code for characteristics, with no link to proteins.

text: DNA molecules carry the genetic code for [lipids|proteins].
opts: proteins
lipids
ribosomal subunits
why: DNA carries the genetic code for proteins. The option “ribosomal subunits” is linked to the nucleolus, where these subunits are made.

q: In the nucleus, we observe a region where the larger and smaller ribosomal subunits are made. What is this region called?
why: The nucleolus is a region inside the nucleus where the larger and smaller ribosomal subunits are made. It is not the whole nucleus, which contains most of the DNA.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: The site where the larger ribosomal subunit is made.
The site where the smaller ribosomal subunit is made.
A matrix with ribosomes and circular DNA molecules.
why: The first three statements describe the nucleolus. A matrix with circular DNA molecules and ribosomes is part of the structure of a mitochondrion.

s: If the larger and smaller ribosomal subunits are made in the nucleus, they are made in the nucleolus.
why: The nucleolus is a region inside the nucleus where both ribosomal subunits are made. The trap is confusing the nucleolus with ribosomes, which carry out protein synthesis.

q: In which part of the mitochondrion would you expect to find circular DNA molecules and ribosomes?
opts: In the space between the outer and inner membranes.
In the matrix, which is surrounded by the folded inner membrane.
On the outer surface of the outer membrane, in the cytoplasm.
In the inner membrane, which is folded and surrounds the matrix.
why: Circular DNA molecules and ribosomes are in the mitochondrial matrix. The trap is confusing the matrix with the inner membrane, which surrounds it and is folded.

s: A mitochondrion is an independent organelle in the cytoplasm with an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane.
why: A mitochondrion is an independent organelle in the cytoplasm, and its inner membrane is folded. The statement does not confuse the position of the mitochondrion with its interior.

text: A mitochondrion has an outer {membrane} and an inner {folded membrane}.
why: The outer membrane surrounds the mitochondrion, while the inner membrane is folded. A “nuclear envelope” surrounds the nucleus, and a smooth membrane does not match the description of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

q: Which organelle has an outer membrane, a folded inner membrane, and a matrix with circular DNA and ribosomes, and is the site of cellular respiration?
why: The description includes the structure of a mitochondrion, where cellular respiration takes place and ATP is produced. Circular DNA and ribosomes are in its matrix.

q: When observing a plant cell, researchers find that the covering outside the plasma membrane has several layers, provides strength and protects against changes in turgor. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
opts: It is a cell wall made of cellulose.
It is a plasma membrane made of cellulose.
It is a cytoskeleton made of cellulose.
It is a cell wall, which animal cells also have.
why: The description matches the plant cell wall, which is outside the membrane and contains several layers of cellulose. The trap is confusing the wall with the membrane or cytoskeleton, or making the false claim that animal cells have cell walls.

s: A cell wall can protect a plant cell against changes in turgor, but animal cells do not have one.
why: In plant cells, the wall helps protect against changes in turgor, while animal cells do not have one. The statement does not claim that animal cells have no other forms of protection.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: Provides strength to the plant cell
A network of proteins in the form of threads or tubes
why: The first three options describe the cell wall. A network of proteins in the form of threads or tubes is characteristic of the cytoskeleton.

q: When analysing the multilayered covering of a plant cell, researchers find that it is made of a polysaccharide that gives the cell strength. Which polysaccharide did they detect?
why: The multiple layers of a plant cell wall are made of the polysaccharide cellulose. A common trap is confusing it with the proteins that make up the cell skeleton.

q: When observing a cell structure, researchers find a green pigment among the many pigments in the thylakoid membrane. Which term best fits this description?
opts: Starch granules, which store starch.
Chlorophyll, the green pigment in the membrane.
Centrioles, structures near the nucleus.
Ribosomes, made of RNA and proteins.
why: The green pigment among the pigments in the thylakoid membrane is chlorophyll. Starch granules are involved in storing starch, not in functioning as a pigment.

s: Chlorophyll is a specialised plastid that enables the cell to store starch.
why: Chlorophyll is the green pigment among the pigments in the thylakoid membrane. The specialised plastids that store starch are starch granules.

text: There are many pigments in the thylakoid membrane, especially the [starchy|green] pigment chlorophyll.
opts: green
specialised
nuclear
why: Chlorophyll is a green pigment, so the word “starchy” should be replaced with “green”. The trap is confusing the pigment with starch granules, which are plastids that store starch.

q: Researchers identify structures in a cell that are specialised plastids for storing a particular substance. Which term matches this finding?
opts: Chlorophyll, the green pigment in the membrane.
Starch granules, plastids that store starch.
Centrioles, structures near the nucleus.
Lysosomes, structures containing digestive enzymes.
why: The description matches starch granules, whose role is to store starch. Chlorophyll is a pigment, while the other two terms refer to different cell structures.

s: If starch granules are present in a cell, they are green pigments in the thylakoid membrane.
why: Starch granules are specialised plastids for storing starch. The green pigment in the thylakoid membrane is chlorophyll, so the statement confuses the two terms.

q: What are the specialised plastids whose role is to store starch called?
why: Starch granules are specialised plastids for storing starch. Chlorophyll is a pigment, not the name of a plastid that stores starch.

q: Which statement correctly links the location and role of centrioles?
opts: They are in the cytoplasm near the nucleus and are involved in cell division.
They are in the nucleus near the chromatin and help store starch.
They are in the thylakoid membrane and are involved in cell division.
They are in the cytoplasm near the nucleus and store water and pigments.
why: Centrioles are in the cytoplasm near the nucleus and are involved in cell division. The thylakoid membrane is associated with chlorophyll, while water and pigments are stored in vacuoles.

s: Centrioles are present in all plant cells.
why: Centrioles are present in animal cells, but in plants they occur only in some cells of lower plants. The trap is generalising this to all plant cells.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: Structures in the cytoplasm near the nucleus.
why: The first three statements describe centrioles. Starch is stored by starch granules, not centrioles.

q: What are the structures in the cytoplasm near the nucleus that are involved in cell division called?
why: Centrioles are in the cytoplasm near the nucleus and take part in cell division. Starch granules, which store starch, do not fit this description.

q: When observing a cell, researchers find a layer around it that gives it shape and protection and regulates the movement of substances into and out of it. Which description best summarises its role?
opts: It surrounds the cell and controls the movement of substances in both directions.
It determines the position of organelles and allows the cell to change shape.
It surrounds the cell on the outside of the membrane and gives it strength.
It enables the cell to move because it projects into its surroundings.
why: The description combines the roles of the cell membrane, which surrounds the cell, gives it shape and protection, and controls the movement of substances. The position of organelles and cell movement are roles of the cell skeleton and cilia and flagella, respectively.

s: If a membrane surrounds a cell but does not control the movement of substances, it performs all the functions of the membrane listed in the learning material.
why: As well as surrounding the cell, the membrane controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell and gives it shape and protection. The statement leaves out important functions.

text: The cell membrane is [completely|selectively] permeable.
opts: selectively
fluid
active
why: The membrane is semi permeable, or selectively permeable, so it does not allow all substances through without control. The trap is confusing selective permeability with complete permeability.

q: Which arrangement of phospholipids is consistent with the fluid mosaic model?
opts: The hydrophobic tails face the surroundings of the cell.
The hydrophobic tails face the inside of the bilayer.
The hydrophobic tails are grouped on only one side of the bilayer.
The hydrophobic tails face the proteins outside the membrane.
why: In a phospholipid bilayer, the hydrophobic tails face inwards. Reversing the direction of the tails is a common trap.

s: In the fluid mosaic model, the lipid bilayer is quite fluid and membrane proteins float in it.
