why: These are characteristics of the fluid mosaic model. The statement does not claim that the proteins are fixed in the bilayer.

q: Which one does not belong, if all the other options describe features of the fluid mosaic model?
items: The lipid bilayer is quite fluid.
why: Microtubules are part of the cell skeleton, while the other options describe the structure or properties of the membrane according to the fluid mosaic model.

text: In the fluid mosaic model, membrane {proteins} can be involved in {active transport}.
why: Membrane proteins can be involved in active transport. Cellulose is listed as a component of the plant cell wall, while cell movement is not a role of membrane proteins in the learning material.

q: A researcher wants to describe the membrane in a way that takes account of both its structure and its fluid nature. Which description is most suitable?
opts: The membrane consists of microtubules floating in a phospholipid bilayer.
The membrane consists of a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins float.
The membrane consists of a fixed phospholipid bilayer surrounded by proteins.
The membrane consists of proteins in which a phospholipid bilayer floats.
why: The fluid mosaic model describes a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins float. Microtubules are not part of the membrane, and the phospholipid bilayer is not fixed.

q: What is the property of the membrane that enables it to control the movement of substances into and out of the cell called?
why: The membrane is semi permeable, or selectively permeable. This is not the same as complete permeability or the fluid nature of the lipid bilayer.

q: When describing the membrane, a student claims that proteins in it can be involved in active transport. Which assessment of the claim is consistent with the material?
opts: The claim is correct, because membrane proteins can be involved in active transport.
The claim is incorrect, because only phospholipids are involved in active transport.
The claim is incorrect, because proteins in the membrane determine the position of organelles.
The claim is correct, because proteins form the entire lipid bilayer.
why: Membrane proteins can be involved in active transport. The trap is to attribute their role to phospholipids or the cytoskeleton.

q: In a cell being observed, a researcher identifies a network of proteins made up of filaments and tubes. Which set of names matches the components of this network?
opts: Microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules
Microfilaments, the cell membrane and microtubules
Intermediate filaments, cilia and the cell wall
Microtubules, flagella and intermediate filaments
why: The three types of components of the cytoskeleton are microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules. Cilia and flagella are made of microtubules, but they are not the name of one of the three types of cytoskeletal components.

s: If a cell changes shape, the cytoskeleton is not involved, since its role is limited to supporting organelles.
why: As well as supporting organelles, the cytoskeleton also enables the cell to change shape. The trap is to present one of its roles as if it were the only one.

s: The cytoskeleton is a network of proteins that can form filaments or tubes.
why: This matches the structure of the cytoskeleton. The statement does not limit its components to filaments or to tubes alone.

q: In a cell, its shape changes and its organelles move at the same time. Which explanation best links these observations to the cytoskeleton?
opts: The cytoskeleton can change the shape of the cell and determine the position of organelles
The cytoskeleton can surround the cell and control the movement of substances across it
The cytoskeleton can protect the cell from changes in turgor and provide strength
The cytoskeleton can enable active transport and the movement of membrane proteins
why: The cytoskeleton enables the cell to change shape, supports organelles and determines their position. The other options describe roles of the membrane or cell wall.

s: Cilia and flagella can be present in animal cells, and in plant cells only in some unicellular algae.
why: The statement correctly distinguishes between animal cells and some plant cells. The trap would be to generalise that they are present in all plant cells.

q: A moving animal cell and a moving plant cell that is a unicellular alga were observed in a sample. Which conclusion about cilia or flagella is consistent with the material?
opts: They can be present in both of the cells observed
They can be present only in the plant cell
They can be present only in the animal cell
They can be present in all plant cells
why: Cilia and flagella are present in animal cells and in some plant cells, including some unicellular algae. The incorrect conclusion is that they are characteristic of all plant cells.

text: Cilia and flagella are made of {microtubules} and are anchored in the {cell membrane}.
why: Cilia and flagella are made of microtubules and anchored in the cell membrane. The trap is to confuse microtubules with another type of component, or the membrane with the cell wall.

q: Which one does not belong?
items: Changing the shape of the cell
why: Microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules are components of the cytoskeleton. Changing the shape of the cell is one of its roles, not a type of component.

q: A cell maintains its shape, while its organelles have a defined position inside it. Which statement best explains how these observations relate to the cytoskeleton?
opts: The cytoskeleton maintains the shape of the cell and determines the position of organelles
The cytoskeleton controls the movement of substances across the cell and determines the position of organelles
The cytoskeleton protects against changes in turgor and maintains the shape of the cell
The cytoskeleton enables the cell to move and controls the movement of substances across it
why: Maintaining the cell's shape and determining the position of organelles are roles of the cytoskeleton. Control of the movement of substances across the cell is a role of the cell membrane, while protection against changes in turgor is a role of the cell wall.

q: A cell in a sample has neither a cellulose cell wall nor chloroplasts. Which classification also matches the information that the cell is heterotrophic?
opts: An animal cell, because it is heterotrophic.
A plant cell, because it is heterotrophic.
An animal cell, because it is autotrophic.
A plant cell, because it is autotrophic.
why: Animal cells are heterotrophic and do not have a cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts. The trap is to confuse the modes of nutrition of plant and animal cells.

q: In a comparison of two cell types, cells of type X are autotrophic, while cells of type Y are heterotrophic. Which classification fits this comparison?
opts: X are animal cells and Y are plant cells.
X are plant cells and Y are animal cells.
X and Y are plant cells.
X and Y are animal cells.
why: Plant cells are autotrophic, while animal cells are heterotrophic. The trap is to confuse these two modes of nutrition.

q: A group of cells is observed to have irregular shapes. Which conclusion is consistent with the material?
opts: They are plant cells, because they have irregular shapes.
They are animal cells, because they have irregular shapes.
They are plant cells, because they have regular shapes.
They are animal cells, because they have regular shapes.
why: Animal cells do not have regular shapes, whereas plant cells do. The trap is to confuse the characteristic shapes of the two cell types.

q: Which comparison correctly links the cell wall and vacuoles in the two cell types?
opts: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and vacuoles, while animal cells have a cell wall and vacuoles in only some cells.
Plant cells do not have a cellulose cell wall and have vacuoles, while animal cells have a cell wall and vacuoles in only some cells.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and vacuoles, while animal cells do not have a cell wall and have vacuoles in only some cells.
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, but only some have vacuoles, while all animal cells have vacuoles.
why: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and vacuoles, while animal cells do not have a cellulose cell wall and have vacuoles only in some cells. The trap is to confuse the presence of a cell wall or to claim that all animal cells have vacuoles.

s: Plant cells have vacuoles, while vacuoles are found in only some animal cells.
why: The statement matches the difference between plant and animal cells. The trap would be to generalise that animal cells do not have vacuoles or that they all have them.

s: According to the material, if a cell is heterotrophic, it is an animal cell and not a plant cell.
why: Animal cells are heterotrophic, while plant cells are autotrophic. The trap is to confuse these two modes of nutrition.

q: Which characteristic does not belong among the listed characteristics of an animal cell?
items: It does not have a cellulose cell wall.
why: Animal cells do not have regular shapes, so having a regular shape is not one of their characteristics. This is characteristic of plant cells.

q: Which statement does not belong among the correct statements about cell shapes?
items: Animal cells do not have regular shapes.
Plant cells do not have regular shapes.
why: Plant cells have regular shapes, so the statement that they do not have regular shapes is incorrect. The trap is to confuse the description of plant cells with that of animal cells.

q: How are plant cells described in terms of nutrition?
why: Plant cells are autotrophic, while animal cells are heterotrophic. The trap is to choose the term that applies to animal cells.

s: A length of 0.6 µm is equal to 600 nm.
why: One micrometre is 1,000 nanometres, so 0.6 µm is equal to 600 nm. It would be incorrect to use the conversion between millimetres and micrometres.

q: Which notation does not represent the same length as the other three?
why: One millimetre is 1000 micrometres or 1 000 000 nanometres. One thousand nanometres is one micrometre.

q: What do we call the instrument used to observe an object that cannot be seen with the naked eye?
why: A microscope is used to observe objects that cannot be seen with the naked eye.

q: A student wants to observe an object that cannot be seen with the naked eye. Which piece of equipment is suitable for this purpose?
opts: Stage
Microscope
Fine focus knob
Light source
why: We use a microscope to observe objects that cannot be seen with the naked eye. The other terms refer to parts of a microscope.

s: If an object cannot be seen with the naked eye, observing it with a microscope is consistent with the purpose of this instrument.
why: A microscope is an instrument for observing objects that cannot be seen with the naked eye. The statement does not confuse a microscope with its individual parts.

q: Which statement correctly links the people who made the first microscope?
opts: Robert Hooke made it around 1590.
Hans and Zacharias Janssen made it around 1590.
Anton van Leeuwenhoek made it around 1590.
Ernst Ruska made it around 1590.
why: The first microscope is thought to have been made by Hans and Zacharias Janssen around 1590. Hooke coined the word cell, while Ruska later used electrons.

text: In [1665|1931], Ernst Ruska used electrons for the first TEM.
why: Ruska used electrons for the first TEM in 1931. The year 1665 is linked to Hooke's publication of Micrographia, while 1938 is linked to an improved TEM.

s: In 1665, Robert Hooke published Micrographia and coined the word cell.
why: Both links in the statement are correct. A possible trap would be confusing Hooke with the Janssens or Ruska.

q: Who made excellent microscopes?
why: The material links the making of excellent microscopes with Anton van Leeuwenhoek. The first microscope is thought to have been made by the Janssens.

q: Which set contains only parts listed in the notes on the light microscope?
opts: Eyepiece, tube, revolving nosepiece, stage
Condenser, diaphragm, objectives, stage
Eyepiece, condenser, arm, fine focus knob
Light source, diaphragm, specimen, objectives
why: All four terms in the selected set appear in the list of parts. The condenser and diaphragm are mentioned in related material, but not in the list referred to in the question.

q: Which term is not listed among the parts of the light microscope in the notes?
why: The condenser is mentioned in related material, but it is not among the parts listed in the notes for this term. The other three terms are on the list.

s: The eyepiece, objectives, arm, specimen and base are all listed as parts of the light microscope.
why: All five terms are included in the list provided. A possible trap would be confusing them with related terms such as the condenser and diaphragm, which are not listed here.

q: A student has focused the image roughly and now wants to focus it precisely. Which sequence of knobs should they use?
opts: Fine focus knob first, then coarse focus knob
Coarse focus knob first, then fine focus knob
Use the coarse focus knob twice
Use the fine focus knob twice
why: The coarse focus knob is used for rough focusing, while the fine focus knob is used for precise focusing. Reversing the sequence swaps their roles.

s: If the image only needs to be focused precisely, the coarse focus knob is more suitable because it allows rough focusing.
why: Use the fine focus knob for precise focusing and the coarse focus knob for rough focusing. The statement swaps the roles of the knobs.

q: Which knob do you use when the image is already roughly focused and you want to focus it more precisely?
why: Use the fine focus knob for precise focusing. The coarse focus knob is used for rough focusing.

q: The eyepiece magnifies 12× and the objective 25×. What is the total magnification?
why: Multiply the magnifications of the eyepiece and objective: 12 × 25 = 300. Adding the factors would give the wrong answer, 37×.

s: An eyepiece with 8× magnification and an objective with 50× magnification give the same total magnification as a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective.
why: Both combinations give 400×, since 8 × 50 = 10 × 40. The trap is focusing on the different individual factors rather than their product.

text: An eyepiece with 12× magnification and an objective with 25× magnification give a total magnification of [37×|300×].
why: The total magnification is found by multiplying the factors, so 12 × 25 = 300×. The value 37× results from adding them incorrectly.

q: Which calculation gives a different total magnification from the other three?
why: The first three calculations give 400×, while the last gives 300×. The total magnification is found by multiplying the eyepiece and objective factors.

q: A student is classifying microscope parts according to their functions. Which classification is correct?
opts: The eyepiece and objectives form the image, while the base and arm support the microscope.
The eyepiece and arm form the image, while the objectives and base support the microscope.
The condenser and base form the image, while the light and arm support the microscope.
The stage and objectives form the image, while the diaphragm and tube support the microscope.
why: The eyepiece and objectives are optical parts, while the base and arm are mechanical parts. The trap is confusing the optical function of parts with their mechanical function.

s: The condenser with diaphragm is a mechanical part because it supports and moves the microscope.
why: The condenser with diaphragm is an optical part because it helps illuminate the image. Mechanical parts support and move the microscope.

q: Which part is not one of the optical parts of a microscope?
why: The eyepiece, objective lens and diaphragm are optical parts. The stage is a mechanical part that holds the specimen.

q: A student wants to name three mechanical parts that support or move the microscope. Which set is correct?
opts: Base, arm and stage
Light, tube and revolving nosepiece
Eyepiece, objective lens and diaphragm
Condenser, stage and objective lens
why: The base, arm and stage are mechanical parts. Each of the other sets includes at least one optical part or a part that is not mechanical.

q: In which pair is the Slovenian name of a microscope part matched incorrectly with its English name?
why: Revolver is called revolving nosepiece in English, while diaphragm means zaslonka. The other pairs are matched correctly.

q: What is the English name for the microscope tube?
why: The English name for tubus is eyepiece tube. Do not confuse it with eyepiece, which means okular.

text: The English name for the coarse focus knob is [fine focus adjustment knob|coarse focus adjustment knob].
opts: coarse focus adjustment knob
fine focus adjustment knob
objective lens
why: The correct English name is coarse focus adjustment knob. Fine focus adjustment knob means mikrometrski vijak.

q: You move a specimen to the left under the microscope. In which direction does its image move?
opts: To the right, because the image moves in the opposite direction to the specimen.
To the left, because the image moves in the same direction as the specimen.
Upwards, because the image always moves at right angles to the specimen.
Downwards, because the image always flips left and right.
why: The image moves in the opposite direction to the specimen, so when the specimen moves to the left, the image moves to the right. The trap is assuming that the image follows the specimen.

s: If the top of the letter F on the specimen is at the top, it will also be at the top in the image under the microscope.
why: The image is rotated by 180°, so the top is at the bottom and the left is on the right. The trap is to consider only the left to right reversal.

text: When we move the specimen {downwards}, its image moves {upwards}.
why: The image moves in the opposite direction to the specimen, so moving the specimen downwards makes the image move upwards. The trap is choosing the same direction for both movements.

s: If two crossed hairs are at different heights, at high magnification we can use the fine focus knob to focus on either one.
why: At high magnification, the microscope focuses on only one plane. A hair at a different height must therefore be focused on separately.

q: Which knob do you use to shift focus from one crossed hair to the other at high magnification?
why: The fine focus knob makes small adjustments to the focus and lets us focus on a hair at a different height. The trap is choosing the coarse focus knob, which is for rough focusing.

q: At 40×, the objective lens is very close to the cover slip. What could happen if you use the coarse focus knob to focus?
opts: The objective lens could hit the cover slip and damage the glass or lens.
The objective lens could move so far away that the specimen disappears from the field of view.
The cover slip could move because the objective lens increases the working distance.
The image could flip because the coarse focus knob changes the direction of observation.
why: A high magnification objective lens is longer and close to the specimen, so the coarse focus knob could push it into the cover slip. The danger is not related to flipping the image or increasing the working distance.

s: Because a high magnification objective lens is longer and closer to the specimen, we use only the fine focus knob to focus at this magnification.
why: The small working distance means that the objective lens could hit the cover slip if the coarse focus knob is used. The fine focus knob allows precise focusing.

q: Which statement is not a precaution when using a high magnification objective lens?
items: The objective lens is longer than at a lower magnification.
The objective lens is close to the specimen when the image is in focus.
Use only the fine focus knob to focus.
The coarse focus knob can be used to focus roughly and safely.
why: At high magnification, we do not use the coarse focus knob, as the objective lens could hit the cover slip. The first three statements match the information about the objective lens and focusing.

q: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 4× objective lens. What is the total magnification?
why: We get the total magnification by multiplying the magnification of the eyepiece and objective lens, so 10× · 4× = 40×. Adding them would give the wrong result.

q: The eyepiece magnifies 10× and the image is magnified 400×. What is the magnification of the objective lens used?
why: We get the total magnification by multiplying the magnification of the eyepiece and objective lens. Dividing 400× by 10× shows that the objective lens magnifies 40×.

text: A 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective lens give a total magnification of [100×|400×].
why: The magnifications of the eyepiece and objective lens are multiplied, so the total magnification is 10× · 40× = 400×. The trap is choosing 100×, which is the result for a 10× eyepiece and a 10× objective lens.

q: Which statement does not match the observation of crossed hairs at high magnification?
items: The hairs may be at different heights.
The microscope focuses on only one plane.
Depth of field is very small at high magnification.
Focusing on one hair makes both hairs sharp at the same time.
why: Since the hairs are at different heights, they lie in different planes and are not sharp at the same time. We use the fine focus knob to focus on one hair or the other.

text: At high magnification, use the [coarse focus|fine focus] knob to focus.
opts: coarse focus
fine focus
revolving nosepiece
why: At high magnification, we use the fine focus knob because the objective lens is close to the specimen and could hit the cover slip if the coarse focus knob is used. The revolving nosepiece is not a focusing knob.

q: At 400×, the diameter of the field of view is 420 µm. You count 12 cells across its diameter. What is the approximate length of one cell?
opts: 35 µm
42 µm
50 µm
60 µm
why: Divide the diameter of the field of view by the number of cells across it: 420 µm / 12 = 35 µm. The trap is to multiply the number of cells by the diameter instead of dividing it.

s: If an onion epidermis cell is a plant cell, chloroplasts must be visible inside it.
why: There are no chloroplasts in the onion cells being observed. The trap is assuming that chloroplasts are visible in all plant cells.

q: An onion cell is about 200 µm long, while a moss cell is about 45 µm long. Which comparison is most accurate?
opts: A moss cell is about four times longer.
An onion cell is about four times longer.
An onion cell is about four times shorter.
The two cells are about the same length.
why: 200 µm is about four times as much as 45 µm. The trap is mixing up which of the two cells is longer.

text: At 400×, the {diameter of the field of view} is 420 µm. If we count 7 cells across it, one cell is about {60 µm} long.
why: Estimate cell size by dividing the diameter of the field of view by the number of cells across it: 420 µm / 7 = 60 µm. The trap is choosing the wrong division or the wrong number of cells.

q: Which detail does not belong in a description of the observed onion epidermal cells?
items: The cells are elongated and regular in shape.
A cell wall and a nucleus are visible in the cells.
A vacuole is visible in the cells.
Green chloroplasts are visible in the cells.
why: A cell wall, nucleus and vacuole are visible in onion cells, but chloroplasts are not. The trap is generalising that all plant cells have visible chloroplasts.

text: In moss cells, photosynthesis takes place in the [cell wall|chloroplasts].
opts: chloroplasts
cell wall
cytoplasm
why: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts. The trap is confusing chloroplasts with the cell wall, which is also visible in these cells.

q: What do we call the distance across the visible area of a microscope, which we divide by the number of cells across that distance when estimating cell size?
a: diameter of the field of view
why: To calculate cell size, we use the diameter of the field of view and divide it by the number of cells counted across the diameter. The trap is confusing the diameter of the field of view with the microscope's magnification.

s: Green chloroplasts, a cell wall and cytoplasm are visible in moss cells.
why: All three of these structures are visible in moss cells. The trap would be to confuse this plant with onion epidermal cells, which do not have chloroplasts.

q: Under a microscope, you see elongated, regular cells about 200 µm long, with a visible cell wall, nucleus and vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Which specimen are you observing?
opts: Onion bulb scale epidermis.
Moss cells.
Cells that carry out photosynthesis.
Cells about 45 µm long.
why: The description matches onion epidermal cells, which are about 200 µm long and have no visible chloroplasts. The trap is confusing them with moss cells, which are shorter and contain chloroplasts.

q: You notice green structures in moss cells, which are listed as a characteristic component of these cells. Which process takes place in them?
opts: Image formation in a microscope.
Coarse focusing.
Fine focusing.
Photosynthesis.
why: The green structures are chloroplasts, where photosynthesis takes place. The trap is choosing a process related to how a microscope works instead of a process in the cell.

q: On a poster about the origin of the word biology, the Greek terms BIOS and LOGOS are written. Which explanation of their meanings is correct?
opts: BIOS means science, while LOGOS means life.
BIOS means life, while LOGOS means science or study.
BIOS means organism, while LOGOS means environment.
BIOS means nature, while LOGOS means development.
why: BIOS means life, while LOGOS means science or study. The trap is swapping the meanings of the two Greek terms.

s: Biology differs from other natural sciences because it studies only animals, and not other living organisms.
why: Biology is the natural science of life and all living organisms. The statement wrongly limits its subject to animals alone.

q: What is the name of the natural science that covers life and all living organisms?
why: Biology studies life and all living organisms, not just one group of organisms.

q: An organism is recorded as carrying out metabolism, growth, development, reproduction and responses to its environment. Which explanation best links these observations?
opts: These are life processes that organisms can carry out because they are alive.
These are life processes that allow organisms to grow only.
These are features of the environment that allow organisms to reproduce.
These are characteristics of organisms that replace metabolism.
why: Life is a characteristic of organisms that enables them to carry out these life processes. The trap is limiting this to just one process or attributing the characteristics to the environment.

s: Growth and development are life processes, even if an observer does not notice them at the same time as an organism's response to its environment.
why: Life processes include growth, development and responses to the environment. The statement does not say that these processes must occur at the same time.

text: Life is a characteristic of the [environment|organisms] that enables life processes to take place.
opts: organisms
environment
life processes
why: Life is a characteristic of organisms, not the environment. The trap is confusing what has the characteristic with the environment to which the organism responds.

q: A researcher compares botany, zoology and physiology. Which broader branch of biology do all three belong to?
opts: Cell biology.
Environmental and evolutionary biology.
Organismal biology.
Cell and environmental biology.
why: Botany, zoology and physiology are listed as branches of organismal biology. The trap is classifying physiology by the fact that it studies how things function, rather than by the branch it belongs to.

q: Which of the following sciences does not belong to the same broader branch as the others?
why: Cytology, genetics and biochemistry belong to cell biology, while mycology belongs to organismal biology. The trap is that all four are biological sciences, but they do not belong to the same branch.

q: What is the name of the broader branch of biology that includes ecology, evolutionary biology, systematics, biogeography and ethology?
why: All the sciences listed are classified as environmental and evolutionary biology. They do not belong to organismal biology, even though some study living things.

s: Mycology and zoology belong to different broader branches of biology: the former belongs to organismal biology, while the latter belongs to cell biology.
why: Mycology and zoology both belong to organismal biology. The incorrect part of the statement is classifying zoology as cell biology.

q: Methylene blue is added to one of two identical samples of the lining of the mouth. What difference would you expect to see when observing them?
opts: The nucleus will be more visible, but the cell shape will not change.
The cell wall will be more visible, but the cell shape will not change.
The cytoplasm will be more visible, and the cells will have a more regular shape.
The plasma membrane will be more visible, and the cells will have a fixed shape.
why: Methylene blue makes the nucleus visible, but does not change the shape of the cells. The trap is attributing an effect on the cell wall or cell shape to the stain.

s: If an observed cell has a more regular shape because of a cell wall, it is more likely to be a plant cell than an animal cell, according to the course material.
why: Plant cells have a cell wall, which gives them a fixed shape and support. Animal cells have no cell wall and are irregular in shape.

q: Cells obtained by rubbing a cotton bud against the inside of the cheek, then staining the sample with methylene blue.
why: A sample from the inside of the cheek contains cheek cells. The description of the procedure helps identify the sample, rather than merely listing its visible parts.

q: Which statement is not a correct link between plant cells and the cell wall?
items: Because of the cell wall, they have more regular shapes.
The cell wall gives them a fixed shape.
They do not have a cell wall and have irregular shapes.
why: The first three statements describe plant cells. The last describes animal cells, which do not have a cell wall.

text: Methylene blue makes the {nucleus} easier to see; cheek cells do not have a {cell wall}.
why: The stain makes the nucleus visible, while cheek cells do not have a cell wall. The cytoplasm and plasma membrane are visible, but do not fit the missing parts of the sentence.

text: Animal cells [have a cell wall|do not have a cell wall].
opts: do not have a cell wall
have a cell wall
have a fixed shape
why: The correct statement is that animal cells do not have a cell wall. The trap is confusing them with plant cells, which do have a cell wall.

q: When observing stained cells from the inside of the cheek, a pupil sees irregular shapes, a cell outline and a stained inner part. Which explanation is correct?
opts: The inner part is the nucleus, the outline is the plasma membrane, and there is no cell wall.
The inner part is the cytoplasm, the outline is the cell wall, and there is no nucleus.
The inner part is the nucleus, the outline is the cell wall, and there is no plasma membrane.
The inner part is the plasma membrane, the outline is the cytoplasm, and there is no cell wall.
why: Methylene blue makes the nucleus visible. The plasma membrane and cytoplasm are also visible in cheek cells, which do not have a cell wall. The trap is confusing the plasma membrane with the cell wall.

q: A group of researchers works in cytology, genetics and biochemistry. Which broad branch of biology do these subjects belong to?
opts: Organismal biology
Environmental and evolutionary biology
Cell biology
Organismal sciences
why: Cytology, genetics and biochemistry belong to the branch of cell biology. The trap is that genetics and biochemistry may sound like separate broad branches, but in this material they are included here.

q: Which subject does not belong to the same group as the others?
why: Cytology, genetics and molecular biology are subjects that study cells, while botany studies plants. The trap is that all four are part of biology, but they do not belong to the same group.

q: A researcher compares the structure and function of cells in samples with different characteristics. Which subject studies cells, including their structure and function?
why: Cytology studies cells, their structure and their function. The trap is confusing it with the broader branch of cell biology.

q: A researcher first describes the structure of an organism's parts, then observes how they function. Which subject relates to the first part of the research?
opts: Physiology
Anatomy
Zoology
Microbiology
why: Anatomy studies structure, while physiology studies function. The trap is that both subjects relate to the study of organisms, but they differ in what they investigate.

s: If a researcher studies fungi, they are working in microbiology.
why: Fungi are studied by mycology, while microbiology studies microorganisms. The statement confuses the names of two related subjects.

q: A research group focuses on the study of fungi. Which subject is central to their research?
why: Mycology studies fungi. The trap is confusing it with microbiology, which studies microorganisms.

text: Ecology studies the relationships between {living things} and their {environment}.
why: Ecology is concerned with relationships between living things and their environment. The other terms relate to different biological topics, but do not define ecology.

q: Which subject does not belong to the same group as the others?
why: Ecology, ethology and systematics belong to the group of subjects concerned with the environment, evolution and behaviour, while physiology studies how organisms function. The trap is that all the subjects listed study the living world, but they do not belong to the same group.

q: A researcher observes how animals behave in different circumstances. Which subject studies animal behaviour?
why: Ethology studies animal behaviour. The trap is confusing it with ecology, which studies relationships between living things and their environment.

q: A researcher sorts organisms into groups and gives them names. Which subject deals directly with this work?
opts: Ecology
Systematics
Ethology
Physiology
why: Systematics and taxonomy classify and name organisms. The trap is choosing ecology, which studies the relationships between organisms and their environment, not their classification.

q: A researcher compares how the immune system responds in different organisms. Which subject are they using?
opts: Immunology, because it studies the immune system.
Parasitology, because it studies the immune system.
Biotechnology, because it studies the immune system.
Ecology, because it studies the immune system.
why: Immunology studies the immune system. Parasitology studies parasites, while biotechnology uses biological processes to develop useful products and technologies.

q: A research group uses biological processes to develop useful products and technologies. Which subject are they using?
why: Biotechnology uses biological processes to develop useful products and technologies. The trap is that this is not the study of the immune system or parasites.

s: Parasitology studies the immune system, while immunology studies parasites.
why: The statement reverses the meaning of the two subjects. Immunology studies the immune system, while parasitology studies parasites.

q: A researcher observes how a change in water availability affects plants, fish and birds in a pond. Which branch of biology best fits their work?
opts: Ecology, because it investigates the relationships between living things and their environment.
Systematics, because it investigates the relationships between living things and their environment.
Cytology, because it investigates the relationships between living things and their environment.
Parasitology, because it investigates the relationships between living things and their environment.
why: Changes affecting several organisms as a result of an environmental factor are part of ecology. Systematics classifies and names organisms, cytology studies cells, and parasitology studies parasites.

text: Identifying and naming an unknown plant using a key is part of {systematics}, while observing plant cells under a microscope is part of {cytology}.
why: When using a key, a researcher identifies and names an organism, so this is systematics. When observing cells, the researcher is studying cells, so this is cytology.

q: Which task is not an example of cell research?
items: Observing cheek cells under a microscope
Observing onion cells under a microscope
Comparing cheek cells and onion cells
Identifying an unknown plant using a key
why: The first three tasks involve observing cells and belong to cytology. Identifying a plant using a key belongs to systematics.

q: Computer analysis of DNA and genomes is an example of biology being linked with computer science. What is this field called?
why: Bioinformatics analyses DNA and genomes, linking biology with computer science. AlphaFold is another example of this link, as it uses AI to predict the 3D structure of proteins.

q: A researcher wants to measure the electrical activity of the brain. Which device is suitable for this purpose?
opts: EEG, because it measures the electrical activity of the brain.
ECG, because it measures the electrical activity of the brain.
A biosensor, because it measures the electrical activity of the brain.
A pacemaker, because it measures the electrical activity of the brain.
why: An EEG measures the electrical activity of the brain. An ECG measures the electrical activity of the heart, while biosensors can detect things such as blood sugar.

q: Which example does not belong with the listed examples of biology being linked with electrical engineering?
items: An ECG, which measures the electrical activity of the heart
An EEG, which measures the electrical activity of the brain
AlphaFold, which uses AI to predict the 3D structure of proteins
why: An ECG, an EEG and a pacemaker are examples of biology being linked with electrical engineering. AlphaFold uses AI to predict protein structure and is an example of biology being linked with computer science.

s: A robot designed to imitate the movement of an animal is an example of biology being linked with mechanical engineering.
why: Robots that imitate the movement of animals are given as an example of biology being linked with mechanical engineering. The electrical activity of organisms is not measured here.

q: The environment changes in a population. Which example best illustrates natural selection?
opts: Organisms with a particular phenotype survive, but have the same number of offspring as others.
Organisms with a particular phenotype have more offspring, but their trait does not ensure survival.
Organisms with a particular phenotype survive and have more offspring than organisms with other phenotypes.
Organisms with different phenotypes survive and have the same number of offspring.
why: Natural selection favours phenotypes that ensure survival and a greater number of offspring. Options that mention only one of these outcomes do not meet both conditions.

s: If organisms with a particular phenotype survive in a given environment but do not have more offspring than organisms with other phenotypes, then according to the description of natural selection this phenotype is advantageous.
why: An advantageous phenotype must ensure both survival and a greater number of offspring. The trap is that the statement takes survival into account only.

q: In an observed population, organisms with a particular phenotype survive in their environment and have more offspring than organisms with other phenotypes. What do we call the process in which the environment favours these organisms?
why: The process in which the environment favours phenotypes that ensure survival and more offspring is called natural selection.

text: In natural selection, the environment favours organisms with phenotypes that ensure survival and a [smaller|greater] number of offspring.
opts: greater
equal
smaller
why: Advantageous phenotypes ensure a greater number of offspring, not a smaller or equal number. The term must also be linked to survival, which is stated correctly in the sentence.

q: Which statement best illustrates a biological concept?
opts: Biology studies life and all living organisms.
A biological concept is a general statement that explains the structure and functioning of the living world.
Life enables organisms to carry out metabolism, grow and respond to their environment.
Evolution is the gradual development of living things from a common ancestor.
why: Biological concepts are general statements that explain the structure and functioning of the living world. The other options describe biology, life processes or evolution.

s: A biological concept is primarily the name of a particular branch of biology, rather than a general statement about the living world.
why: Biological concepts are general statements that explain the structure and functioning of the living world. The trap is confusing a concept with the name of a branch of biology.

q: A researcher wants to explain how the structure of a part of an organism is related to its function. Which fundamental biological concept is most relevant to her question?
opts: An organism exchanges matter and energy with its environment.
Biological systems are regulated by feedback loops.
Structure and function are linked at all levels.
Hereditary information in the form of DNA ensures the continuity of life.
why: The question is directly about the link between structure and function. The exchange of matter and energy and regulation by feedback loops are different concepts.

q: Which term does not belong among the fundamental biological concepts listed?
items: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit.
An organism exchanges matter and energy with its environment.
why: The first three options are fundamental biological concepts listed in the learning material. Natural selection is the mechanism on which evolution is based.

s: Because the cell is the basic structural and functional unit, living systems are not organised at different levels.
why: The cell is the basic unit, but living systems are still organised hierarchically. The statement wrongly concludes that a basic unit rules out levels of organisation.

q: What term describes the regulation of a biological system in which the effect of a process feeds back and contributes to its regulation?
why: Biological systems are regulated by feedback loops. This is not the exchange of matter and energy with the environment, but a way of regulating a system.

q: When explaining changes in living things, researchers find that the environment favours organisms with traits that enable survival and more offspring. Which process is described?
opts: Evolution as the long term development of living things from a common ancestor.
A feedback loop as a way of regulating a biological system.
Natural selection as the mechanism on which evolution is based.
The exchange of matter and energy between an organism and its environment.
why: The description matches natural selection, in which the environment favours organisms with suitable traits. Evolution is a long term process, while natural selection is its mechanism.

s: Evolution is a rapid process in which present day species develop without a common ancestor.
why: Evolution is a long term and gradual process in which living things develop from a common ancestor. The statement gets both the timescale and the origin of species wrong.

q: What do we call the long term and gradual process by which living things develop from a common ancestor into present day species?
why: This description summarises evolution as the long term and gradual development from a common ancestor into present day species. Natural selection is the mechanism on which this process is based.

q: Which option does not describe evolution or its mechanism?
items: The long term and gradual process by which living things develop.
The development of living things from a common ancestor into present day species.
The process on which evolution is based.
Hereditary information in the form of DNA ensures the continuity of life.
why: The first three options describe evolution or natural selection as its mechanism. The last option is another fundamental biological concept, concerning the role of DNA.

q: A student records the colour of the flowers on two plants and measures their size. Which classification of the data is correct?
opts: Colour is qualitative data, while size is quantitative data.
Colour is quantitative data, while size is qualitative data.
Both are qualitative data because they describe the plants.
Both are quantitative data because they are related to the plants.
why: Colour is determined by observation, while size is determined by measurement. The trap is mixing up how the two types of data are obtained.

s: If a researcher records the smell of a sample and measures its temperature, the smell is qualitative data and the temperature is quantitative data.
why: We identify smell by observation and temperature by measurement. The statement correctly links each type of data to how it is obtained.

q: A researcher compares the number of individuals at two sites. How should the data on their number be classified according to how it is obtained?
why: Number is quantitative data because it is obtained by measurement. It is not qualitative data, which is obtained by observation.

q: Which of the following findings fits the definition of a fact?
opts: A well-founded finding about what is or has existed in the past.
An unverified explanation that seems most likely for a problem.
A planned procedure used to solve a problem.
A measured value that is not yet linked to any phenomenon.
why: A fact is a well-founded finding about what is or has existed in the past. The trap is confusing a fact with an unverified explanation of a problem.

q: What do we call any well-founded finding about what is or has existed in the past?
why: Such a well-founded finding is a fact. Data are facts that we link to a particular phenomenon.

s: Data are facts that we link to a particular phenomenon.
why: The statement summarises the link between data and facts. The trap would be to claim that data are not linked to a phenomenon.

q: A student wants to solve a problem systematically and compare the sizes of two samples. Which method directly fits the way they are collecting data?
opts: Measurements, because they are comparing the sizes of samples.
Observation, because size can be identified just by looking.
Experiment, because every comparison of size takes place under controlled conditions.
Fieldwork, because sizes are always determined in the field.
why: Size is quantitative data, which is obtained by measurement. The trap is assuming that every comparison involves an experiment or fieldwork.

q: Which one does not belong?
why: Observation, measurements and experiment are methods of solving a problem. A fact is a well-founded finding, not a method.

text: To identify the colour of a sample, the student uses [measurements|observation].
opts: observation
fieldwork
experiment
why: We identify colour by observation. Measurements are a trap because they are associated with obtaining quantitative data.

q: A researcher studies a fundamental law of nature. When discovered, their findings have no practical value for everyday life. Which branch of science is this?
opts: Applied science, because it studies a phenomenon from nature.
Basic science, because it studies fundamental laws.
Applied science, because its findings are scientific.
Basic science, because its findings are already useful.
why: Basic science studies fundamental laws of nature, and its findings have no practical value when first discovered. The trap is confusing basic science with applied science.

s: If scientific findings have practical value for everyday life, this is applied science.
why: Applied science has findings with practical value for everyday life. The statement does not confuse practical value with the study of fundamental laws in basic science.

q: Which description is different from the other three?
items: It studies fundamental laws of nature, and its findings are not yet useful when discovered.
It studies fundamental laws without its findings being useful when discovered.
Its findings have practical value for everyday life.
When discovered, its findings have no practical value for everyday life.
why: The third description is characteristic of applied science. The other descriptions fit basic science.

q: A researcher has defined the problem and formed a hypothesis. They then collected data. Which stage comes next in the sequence?
opts: Data analysis.
Defining the problem.
Methods of investigation.
Forming a hypothesis.
why: After data collection come methods of investigation, which include observation, measurements, experiment and fieldwork. Data analysis is the next stage.

text: After defining the problem comes the {hypothesis}, and after collecting data come the {methods of investigation}.
why: The hypothesis follows the definition of the problem, and methods of investigation follow data collection. Fieldwork is one of the methods, while data analysis is the final stage.

s: In the sequence of scientific research, data analysis takes place before data collection.
why: Data are collected first and then analysed. The trap is that the stages are in the wrong order.

q: After carrying out the methods, a researcher examines and evaluates the data they have collected. Which stage of research are they carrying out?
why: Data analysis is the stage in which a researcher processes the data collected. They are no longer collecting data or using a method of investigation.

q: Based on known facts, a student suggests the most likely explanation for a problem, but has not yet tested it. What is this suggestion called?
opts: Data, because it relates to a phenomenon.
A method, because it guides the solution to a problem.
A hypothesis, because it is an unverified explanation of a problem.
A fact, because it is based on known findings.
why: A hypothesis is an unverified conclusion based on known facts and is the most likely explanation of a problem. A fact is not simply a suggested, unverified explanation.

s: A hypothesis is an already tested conclusion that has definitively confirmed an explanation of a problem.
why: A hypothesis is an unverified conclusion, not an explanation that has already been tested. The trap is confusing a proposed explanation with a finding made after testing.

q: After defining a problem, a researcher forms an unverified suggestion based on known facts. What is this step in the research process called?
why: A hypothesis, or conjecture, is an unverified explanation of a problem, formed on the basis of known facts. It follows the definition of the problem in the research sequence.

q: A student studies a phenomenon under controlled conditions and describes the procedure precisely. Their classmate then repeats it using the same description. Which feature most directly explains how the classmate can repeat the study?
opts: The phenomenon is studied under controlled conditions.
The procedure is clearly designed and described.
The phenomenon is explained by a widely accepted theory.
The findings have practical value for everyday life.
why: A clear description of the procedure enables someone else to repeat it. Controlled conditions are a feature of an experiment, but on their own they do not ensure that it can be repeated.

s: Studying a phenomenon under controlled conditions is an experiment even if the procedure is not clearly described and therefore cannot be repeated.
why: An experiment must be clearly designed and described so that it can be repeated. Controlled conditions alone are not enough to meet all the key features of an experiment.

q: Which option does not belong if the others describe the characteristics of an experiment?
items: Studying a phenomenon under controlled conditions
A clearly designed and described procedure
The possibility of repeating the procedure
A broad, repeatedly tested and generally accepted explanation
why: The first three options describe the characteristics of an experiment. The last describes a theory, not an experiment.

q: A research explanation has already been proven to be a theory. According to your notes, what do we call it?
opts: Hypothesis
Theory
Law
Experiment
why: A law is a proven theory. A theory is a repeatedly tested and generally accepted explanation, but is not itself described as a proven theory.

q: What do we call an explanation that is broad, repeatedly tested and generally accepted?
why: These are the characteristics of a theory. According to your notes, a law is a proven theory, so it should not be confused with the explanation described here.

s: According to your notes, hypotheses develop into laws, which then develop into theories.
why: The sequence is the other way round: hypotheses develop into theories, and these then develop into laws. A law is a proven theory.

q: An experiment shows that water passes through a membrane, but dissolved substance X does not. Which conclusion best explains the result?
opts: The membrane is selectively permeable, as it allows some substances through but not others.
The membrane is fully permeable, as it allows water through.
The membrane does not allow any substances through, so substance X does not move.
The membrane allows only dissolved substances through, but not water.
why: The membrane allows water through, but not substance X, so it allows different substances through differently. The trap is to conclude that allowing water through means allowing all substances through.

s: If the plasma membrane allows water through, it must also allow all dissolved substances through.
why: The plasma membrane allows water through, but not many dissolved substances. Allowing one kind of substance through does not mean that the membrane allows everything through.

q: What do we call the property of a membrane that allows some substances through but not others?
why: Selective permeability means that the membrane regulates the movement of substances. It does not allow all substances through without distinction.

q: A substance moves through carrier proteins from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, without using energy. Which description fits this example?
opts: Passive transport through carrier proteins.
Active transport through carrier proteins.
Passive transport only through the lipid bilayer.
Active transport through channel proteins.
why: The substance moves from a higher to a lower concentration and no energy is needed, so this is passive transport. Carrier proteins are one of its pathways. The trap is to confuse the type of protein with the direction of movement and energy use.

s: If a substance moves from a lower to a higher concentration, this is passive transport when it moves through a channel protein.
why: Passive transport takes place from a higher to a lower concentration, regardless of whether the substance moves through a channel protein. The statement confuses the direction of passive transport.

q: What do we call transport in which a substance moves from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration without needing energy?
why: Passive transport is characterised by movement from a higher to a lower concentration and does not require energy. Movement through a membrane alone does not determine the type of transport.

q: In an experiment, the surrounding solution has more dissolved substances than the cell. How do we describe it in relation to the cell?
opts: A hypertonic solution.
A hypotonic solution.
A passive solution.
A selectively permeable solution.
why: A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the cell. The trap is to confuse it with a hypotonic solution, which has a lower concentration of dissolved substances.

s: If the surrounding solution has fewer dissolved substances than the cell, it is hypotonic in relation to the cell.
why: A hypotonic solution has a lower concentration of dissolved substances than the cell. What matters is the comparison with the cell, not the concentration of the solution on its own.

q: Which description does not fit a hypertonic solution in relation to the cell?
items: It has a higher concentration of dissolved substances than the cell.
It contains more dissolved substances than the cell.
It has a lower concentration of dissolved substances than the cell.
Its solute concentration is higher than that in the cell.
why: A lower concentration of dissolved substances than the cell describes a hypotonic solution. The other descriptions express that a hypertonic solution has more dissolved substances than the cell.

q: In which example is the stated route of movement a possible form of passive transport?
opts: The substance moves through a channel protein.
The substance moves only from a lower to a higher concentration.
The substance moves through a membrane pump without energy.
The substance moves from a higher to a lower concentration only when energy is used.
why: Movement through channel proteins is one form of passive transport. The trap is to confuse it with active transport, which takes place against the concentration gradient and requires energy.

q: A plant cell is placed in a solution with more dissolved substances than the cell. Which change best describes its response?
opts: The vacuole and protoplast shrink, and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
The vacuole fills with water, and the membrane presses more firmly against the cell wall.
The cell swells and bursts because the cell wall shrinks together with the membrane.
Water enters the cell, increasing the turgor pressure on the cell wall.
why: In a hypertonic environment, water leaves the cell, so the vacuole and protoplast shrink and the membrane pulls away from the wall. The trap is to confuse this with changes in a hypotonic environment.

s: During plasmolysis, the cell wall shrinks together with the contents of the plant cell.
why: Water leaves the cell, so the vacuole and protoplast shrink, while the cell wall remains in place. The incorrect statement confuses the wall with the membrane.

q: What do we call the process in which water loss causes the plant protoplast to shrink and the membrane to pull away from the cell wall?
why: The description includes shrinkage of the cell contents and the membrane pulling away from the wall, which defines plasmolysis. Water leaving the cell alone does not name the whole process.

q: A plant cell that has lost water in a hypertonic solution is moved into a hypotonic solution. What may happen?
opts: Water enters the cell, the vacuole fills, and the cell gradually regains its original shape.
Water leaves the cell, the vacuole shrinks, and the membrane pulls away from the cell wall.
Water enters the cell, but the vacuole remains shrunk and turgor pressure disappears.
Water enters the cell, which swells and bursts because of its rigid cell wall.
why: In a hypotonic environment, water enters the cell and fills the vacuole, so the cell gradually regains its original shape. The option about bursting confuses a plant cell with an animal cell.

s: When water fills the vacuole of a plant cell in a hypotonic environment, the resulting turgor pressure pushes against the cell wall, which prevents the cell from bursting.
why: Water fills the vacuole and exerts pressure on the cell wall, while the rigid wall prevents the cell from bursting. The trap is to assume that swelling must cause the cell to break apart.

q: What process allows a plant cell to gradually regain its original shape after shrinking because of water loss?
why: Deplasmolysis is the reverse of plasmolysis, and during it the cell gradually regains its original shape. Plasmolysis means shrinking as a result of water loss.

q: An animal cell is placed in a hypotonic solution. Which outcome is most likely?
opts: Water enters the cell, which swells and may burst.
Water leaves the cell, which swells and may burst.
Water enters the cell, which shrinks and becomes wrinkled.
Water leaves the cell, which retains its shape because of the cell wall.
why: In a hypotonic environment, water enters an animal cell, which swells and may burst. The traps are reversing the direction in which water moves or attributing a cell wall to an animal cell.

s: In a hypertonic environment, an animal cell loses water and shrinks.
why: In a hypertonic environment, water leaves an animal cell, so it shrinks or becomes wrinkled. The opposite direction would describe the response to a hypotonic environment.

q: Which description does not belong among the outcomes typical of a plant cell in a hypotonic environment?
items: Water enters the cell and the vacuole fills.
Turgor pressure develops and pushes against the cell wall.
The rigid cell wall prevents the cell from bursting.
The cell swells and bursts because it has no cell wall.
why: The description of bursting because there is no cell wall applies to an animal cell, not a plant cell. The other descriptions involve water entering the cell and the protective role of the plant cell wall.

q: Two cells, one plant cell and one animal cell, are in a hypotonic environment. Which explanation best explains why the animal cell may burst but the plant cell does not?
opts: The animal cell has no cell wall, but the plant cell does.
The animal cell has a vacuole, but the plant cell does not.
The plant cell loses water, but the animal cell takes it in.
The plant cell has no membrane, while the membrane protects the animal cell from water.
why: Both cells take in water, but the cell wall protects the plant cell from bursting, while the animal cell has no cell wall. The traps are attributing the difference to the direction in which water moves or to the absence of a membrane.

q: A pupil drew a sketch in pencil, using smooth lines and no shading. They labelled the parts by placing the labels directly on the drawing. What should they change?
opts: They should label each part with a line and place the label next to it.
They should label each part with a colour and place the label next to it.
They should replace the labels with short lines without any text.
They should label the parts with lines and write the magnification next to them.
why: Label parts of a sketch with a line and place the label next to it. Colours, marks without labels and writing the magnification beside the label lines do not follow the instructions.

s: If a pupil shades an area that they actually saw, the sketch is still drawn according to the rules.
why: A sketch should not be shaded, even if the shaded area is visible. The trap is assuming that the rule to draw only what is visible overrides the rule against shading.

q: Below their sketch, a pupil writes how many times larger the image is. What is this information called?
why: Write the magnification below the sketch. Do not confuse it with the label for an individual part, which is placed next to a line.

q: Which action is not one of the rules for making a sketch?
items: Draw the sketch in pencil using smooth lines.
Show only what can be seen in the sketch.
Label the parts with a line and place the label next to it.
Also add parts that cannot be seen if they are expected to be there.
why: A sketch shows only what can be seen, so do not add parts that are expected but cannot be seen. The other options describe rules for drawing and labelling a sketch.

q: A pupil has listened to the teacher's instructions, but has not yet read the instructions for the experiment or prepared the equipment. What should they do before starting?
opts: Read the instructions for the experiment and prepare the necessary equipment and chemicals.
Start the experiment, then check the instructions and find the equipment while working.
Record the expected results, then start the experiment without preparing the equipment.
Dispose of the waste according to the instructions, then read the instructions for the experiment.
why: Before carrying out the experiment, read the instructions and prepare the equipment and chemicals. The trap is starting the experiment before getting ready.

s: We can record the results of an experiment only after disposing of the waste and tidying the work area.
why: Record the results on the worksheet before disposing of the waste and tidying the work area. The statement reverses the order of these steps.

text: Dispose of waste [before|after] checking the instructions.
opts: after
during
without
why: Waste must be disposed of according to the instructions. The trap is choosing a word that suggests disposing of it without following the instructions.

q: A container displays the skull and crossbones pictogram. What hazard does it indicate?
opts: Acute toxicity.
Irritation and harmful effects on health.
Serious health hazards, such as carcinogenicity or mutagenicity.
Hazardous to the environment.
why: The skull and crossbones indicates acute toxicity. The trap is confusing it with other pictograms that also warn of health hazards.

q: Which pictogram indicates a different type of hazard from the other three?
items: Silhouette of a person with a star on the chest.
why: The dead tree and fish indicate a hazard to the environment, while the other pictograms indicate health hazards. The trap is that all four are warning pictograms.

s: The flame over a circle indicates a flammable substance, while the flame alone indicates an oxidising substance.
why: The flame over a circle indicates an oxidising substance, while the flame alone indicates a flammable substance. The statement confuses the meanings of similar pictograms.

q: A pupil has already transferred the specimen into a drop of water on a microscope slide. How should they correctly position the cover slip?
opts: Rest one edge against the drop at a 45° angle and slowly lower the cover slip.
Place the cover slip flat on the drop and then quickly push it across the specimen.
Rest the cover slip against the drop at a 45° angle and quickly drop it onto the specimen.
Place the cover slip under the specimen, then add a drop of water to its centre.
why: Hold the cover slip by its edges, rest one edge against the drop at a 45° angle and lower it slowly. The trap is lowering it quickly, which prevents the drop from spreading evenly.

text: Begin lowering the cover slip at an angle of [90°|45°].
